chunks.title: FleetFlow at a glance
chunks.heading: What FleetFlow is
chunks.text: What FleetFlow is: FleetFlow is Rahul Khanke's logistics dispatch and fleet data-engineering project. It explores vehicle routing, event-driven logistics and operational visibility: from a depot's incoming orders to a route proposal a dispatcher can inspect, and from driver GPS events to a live map and an analytics warehouse. Live demo: https://fleet-flow-rho.vercel.app. Source: https://github.com/HuLaxx/FleetFlow.

chunks.title: FleetFlow at a glance
chunks.heading: Tech stack
chunks.text: - Interface: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, tRPC, MapLibre and deck.gl maps. - API and route planning: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and Google OR-Tools for vehicle routing with capacity and time-window constraints. - Events and telemetry: Kafka (Redpanda in CI), a transactional outbox and inbox, a GPS consumer, WebSockets, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, TimescaleDB and Redis. - Lakehouse: bronze CSV, a data-contract quality gate, a PySpark silver job (idempotent, date-partitioned Parquet) and a dbt star schema that runs on DuckDB and is Snowflake-compatible; orchestrated by an Airflow DAG and deployable to Databricks on Azure with Terraform (ADLS Gen2, Databricks, Key Vault). - Infrastructure and quality: Docker Compose, Kubernetes (kind) manifests, Terraform for Azure and a review-only AWS module, GitHub Actions CI, Playwright browser tests, Prometheus/Grafana-style pipeline observability. - Machine learning: chronological demand-forecasting baselines and route-planning baseline evaluations on synthetic data.

chunks.title: FleetFlow at a glance
chunks.heading: How route planning works
chunks.text: A dispatcher picks a depot and date, FleetFlow loads vehicles and pending orders, OR-Tools models vehicle capacity, depot location, route duration and service windows, and the solver returns candidate routes. The optimize endpoint is a read-only preview; a separate plan endpoint persists a planned route, and approval is a separate, authorised dispatcher decision. A dedicated CI benchmark compares OR-Tools with a capacity- and window-aware greedy baseline on synthetic 8-stop, 12-stop and infeasible cases.

chunks.title: FleetFlow at a glance
chunks.heading: How GPS reaches the map
chunks.text: How GPS reaches the map: An authenticated driver posts GPS events to the FastAPI backend, which writes them through a PostgreSQL outbox to Kafka/Redpanda; a GPS consumer stores positions in PostGIS and pushes them to the browser over WebSockets. This journey passed a non-mocked Chromium CI run with synthetic input on disposable PostGIS and Redpanda services.

chunks.title: FleetFlow at a glance
chunks.heading: What is verified and what is not
chunks.text: Verified in CI with synthetic data: the authenticated GPS to Kafka to PostGIS to WebSocket browser journey; immutable Parquet replay with clean/curated reconciliation; dbt builds with passing data tests; Airflow DAG import and dependency validation; the OR-Tools benchmark; the lakehouse pipeline end to end. Not claimed: a production deployment, real fleet or customer data, live hosted backend behind the public demo, a real Apache Flink job (the event processor is a simplified Python module), or provisioned AWS resources (the AWS Terraform is review-only). Several milestones live in stacked draft pull requests rather than merged code; the evidence register records each one.

chunks.title: GraphGuard at a glance
chunks.heading: What GraphGuard is
chunks.text: GraphGuard is Rahul Khanke's graph-based fraud investigation project. It shows how a suspicious transaction should become a reviewable investigation rather than an automatic fraud verdict: events are ingested, relationships between accounts, devices and merchants are projected into a graph, a model scores the transaction with explanations, and a human analyst reviews the case. All data is synthetic. Demo: https://graph-guard-frontend.vercel.app. Source: https://github.com/HuLaxx/GraphGuard.

chunks.title: GraphGuard at a glance
chunks.heading: Tech stack
chunks.text: - Ingestion: Kafka with Avro and Confluent Schema Registry, a durable first-observed SQLite source ledger. - Graph: Neo4j with Cypher for user, device and merchant relationships; point-in-time (leakage-safe) graph-context features. - Machine learning: scikit-learn logistic regression and XGBoost trained on chronological splits, an MLflow-based release gate, hash-pinned (SHA-256) model and feature artifacts, native XGBoost TreeSHAP explanations, offline calibration and drift monitoring. - Serving and review: Python FastAPI review API with signed short-lived reviewer and admin identities and a keyed local audit chain; a GraphQL demo API. - Frontend: Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, D3 network graph and SHAP charts, Vitest tests. - Delivery: Docker Compose, GitHub Actions CI (including real Kafka/Avro/Schema Registry/Neo4j integration jobs, Chromium analyst/admin review tests, npm audit and a Trivy security scan), review-only Terraform for an opt-in AWS research sandbox.

chunks.title: GraphGuard at a glance
chunks.heading: Model results (synthetic only)
chunks.text: On a deterministic synthetic chronological holdout (720 events, 144 test records, 16 simulated positives), XGBoost reached PR-AUC 0.7650 and ROC-AUC 0.9409, against 0.6887 and 0.9072 for logistic regression. Its realised test false-positive rate was 9.375%, above the 5% budget chosen on validation data, which the model card reports as a limitation. These are synthetic research numbers, not real-world fraud accuracy.

chunks.title: GraphGuard at a glance
chunks.heading: What is verified and what is not
chunks.text: Verified in CI: Avro records through Kafka and Schema Registry into Neo4j, point-in-time features, a hash-pinned model, genuine native SHAP, signed local case review in real Chromium, and dependency security scans. The project scores itself 70/100 on an evidence-weighted release scorecard. Not claimed: production deployment, real or licensed fraud data, enterprise OIDC/MFA, independently anchored audit, production load testing, or provisioned cloud infrastructure. The hosted GraphQL demo is illustrative and is not the signed Python case service.

chunks.title: Sentinance at a glance
chunks.heading: What Sentinance is
chunks.text: What Sentinance is: Sentinance is Rahul Khanke's real-time crypto and market intelligence project. It explores how raw exchange data becomes structured signals, model outputs and AI-assisted analysis, while keeping observed prices, predictions and generated explanations clearly separate. Demo: https://sentinance.vercel.app. Source: https://github.com/HuLaxx/Sentinance.

chunks.title: Sentinance at a glance
chunks.heading: Tech stack
chunks.text: - Frontend: Next.js 16, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vitest and Playwright tests. - APIs and streaming: Python, FastAPI, WebSockets with Redis Pub/Sub, server-sent events, JWT authentication. - Data: versioned Kafka events, a duplicate-safe PostgreSQL price-event ledger, TimescaleDB for price history, immutable checksum-verified Parquet snapshots, dbt models with data-quality tests on DuckDB. - Machine learning: technical indicators, a chronological ridge autoregression forecast compared with last-price and moving-average baselines, and an optional PyTorch LSTM experiment. - AI and retrieval: a LangGraph research agent that only explains a move when it can cite evidence, Gemini and Groq integrations with fallbacks, and Qdrant retrieval evaluated in CI. - Platform: Docker Compose, Kubernetes and monitoring configurations, Prometheus metrics, GitHub Actions CI, review-only Terraform for an AWS S3/Glue/Athena analytics sandbox.

chunks.title: Sentinance at a glance
chunks.heading: How data flows
chunks.text: A source adapter validates aggregate-trade payloads with source-owned IDs, publishes them to Kafka, and a consumer persists them to a PostgreSQL ledger with a unique source/symbol/ID constraint so replays are idempotent. A local source checkpoint and receipt reconciliation detect events that were acknowledged by Kafka but never reached the database and replay them. The ledger exports raw, validated and curated Parquet snapshots that dbt builds into marts; a forecast report is produced from the curated data and cited by the LangGraph evidence path, then shown in the Next.js evidence page.

chunks.title: Sentinance at a glance
chunks.heading: What is verified and what is not
chunks.text: Verified with synthetic data in CI: the fixture source to real Kafka to PostgreSQL to checked Parquet to historical forecast to citation to browser journey; 463 API tests on the reviewed revision; repeated 9-step dbt builds; a Chromium test that rejects a deliberately corrupted model report; offline Terraform validation; a Qdrant retrieval evaluation (dense recall@5 0.979 on a small synthetic corpus). Not claimed: live production price streaming, deployed AWS services, profitable or live forecast accuracy, live LSTM accuracy, full LLM evaluation or real user traffic. The deterministic LangGraph evidence path makes no LLM requests.

chunks.title: FleetFlow lakehouse pipeline
chunks.text:
A batch data platform for FleetFlow's delivery data: bronze → quality gate → silver (PySpark) → gold (dbt star schema), orchestrated by Airflow, deployable to Databricks on Azure with Terraform, and verified end to end in CI.
bronze/ quality.py spark_job.py dbt_warehouse/ raw CSV per table ──▶ contracts, quarantine ──▶ conformed Parquet, ──▶ star schema (DuckDB or (generate.py, and a pass-rate gate dedupe, derived metrics, Snowflake): 5 dims, seeded + defects) (fails the run) partitioned by date incremental fact, KPIs (idempotent overwrite) + 30-odd dbt tests └───────────── Airflow DAG: lakehouse_daily.py (one logical date per run, backfill-safe) ─────────────┘

chunks.title: FleetFlow lakehouse pipeline
chunks.heading: What each part does
chunks.text: Layer · Code · What it provesSynthetic source data · generate.py · Seeded, byte-for-byte reproducible data for 6 tables, with known injected defects (nulls, out-of-range values, unknown keys, invalid statuses, late duplicates). Data contracts + quality gate · quality.py · Schema, type, not-null, accepted-value, range and foreign-key checks; bad rows go to quarantine/ with reasons; late duplicates keep the newest version; the run fails if a table's pass rate drops below the threshold. Silver (PySpark) · spark_job.py · Explicit schemas with FAILFAST, window-based dedupe, derived on-time / lateness / ingest-latency columns, partitioned Parquet with dynamic partition overwrite, so re-runs and backfills never duplicate rows. Runs locally, on Databricks or any Spark 3.5 cluster. Gold (dbt) · ../dbt_warehouse/ · Star schema: dim_date, dim_depot, dim_vehicle, dim_driver, dim_customer, incremental fct_deliveries (unique key + lookback window for late data) and fct_daily_depot_kpis. Same SQL runs on DuckDB (CI) and Snowflake. Tested with unique, not-null, relationship, accepted-value and custom tests. Orchestration · ../airflow/dags/lakehouse_daily.py · Daily DAG, one logical date per run, retries with backoff, ordered backfills.

chunks.title: FleetFlow lakehouse pipeline
chunks.heading: What each part does
chunks.text: Databricks · ../databricks/databricks.yml · Asset bundle that runs the Spark job as a serverless job (Free Edition compatible). Infrastructure · ../../infra/azure-lakehouse/ · Terraform: ADLS Gen2 lake with bronze/silver/gold/quarantine containers, lifecycle policy, Databricks workspace + access connector (managed identity, no storage keys), Key Vault, Log Analytics. CI · ../../.github/workflows/lakehouse.yml · Runs every test (including Spark), the full pipeline, an incremental dbt re-run, a silver-vs-gold reconciliation, terraform validate, and posts the measured results on the PR.

chunks.title: FleetFlow lakehouse pipeline
chunks.heading: Run it locally
chunks.text:
pip install "pyspark==3.5.3" "pandas==2.2.3" "numpy<2" pytest dbt-duckdb duckdb # Java 17 required for Spark export PYTHONPATH=data-engineering
python -m lakehouse.generate --out data/lakehouse --days 30 --orders-per-day 2000 python -m lakehouse.quality --root data/lakehouse --min-pass-rate 0.95 python -m lakehouse.spark_job --root data/lakehouse --start-date 2026-01-01 --end-date 2026-01-30 (cd data-engineering/dbt_warehouse && dbt build --profiles-dir .)
python -m pytest data-engineering/lakehouse/tests -v # Spark tests skip if PySpark is missing python -m lakehouse.benchmark --root data/lakehouse --days 30 --orders-per-day 5000
To run the gold layer on Snowflake instead, set DBT_TARGET=snowflake and the SNOWFLAKE_* variables listed in dbt_warehouse/profiles.yml, and load the silver Parquet into a SILVER schema (for example through an external stage on the ADLS silver container).

chunks.title: FleetFlow lakehouse pipeline
chunks.heading: Known limits
chunks.text: - The Airflow DAG compiles but is not executed in CI (Airflow isn't installed there). - The repo's older Backend Tests workflow was already failing on main before this pipeline was added; it is unrelated to the lakehouse code. - databricks.yml and the Terraform are validated syntactically only; nothing is deployed, so no cloud costs are incurred. - The Snowflake target uses the same SQL as DuckDB but hasn't been run against a live Snowflake account.

chunks.title: Pipeline observability
chunks.text:
Answers three operational questions about FleetFlow's batch pipelines:
1. Did the pipeline run, and did it work? Every task run is recorded (start, finish, duration, rows, error) and exported as Prometheus metrics. 2. Is the source data fresh? dbt source freshness SLAs on the raw tables, with each dbt verdict re-derived independently from the timestamps. 3. Will someone be told? Failed runs and stale sources produce alerts (webhook with retries and de-duplication, or logs), and Prometheus alert rules cover the same conditions plus "the freshness check stopped running".
Standard library only (Python 3.10+), so it runs inside Airflow workers, CI steps and cron jobs without adding dependencies.

No real Slack/Teams/PagerDuty endpoint is configured Airflow callbacks · Wired into daily_optimization and hourly_forecast via an optional import; callbacks are unit-tested with Airflow-shaped contexts, not in a running Airflow

chunks.title: Pipeline observability
chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text:
pip install -e data-engineering/observability
# Wrap any step: records the run, writes metrics, alerts if it fails. python -m fleetflow_observability track --store out/runs.jsonl --alert \ --pipeline dbt --task source_freshness --expected-interval-seconds 3600 \ --metrics-out monitoring/textfile/runs.prom -- \ dbt source freshness --project-dir data-engineering/dbt --output "$PWD/out/sources.json"
# Turn dbt's artifact into metrics, a Markdown summary and alerts; gate on errors. python -m fleetflow_observability freshness --sources-json out/sources.json \ --metrics-out monitoring/textfile/freshness.prom --summary-md out/freshness.md \ --alert --fail-on error
In Python:
from fleetflow_observability import JsonlRunStore, track_run from fleetflow_observability.alerts import dispatcher_from_env
with track_run("daily_optimization", "solve", JsonlRunStore("out/runs.jsonl"), dispatcher_from_env(), expected_interval_seconds=86400) as run: run.rows_out = solve_and_count()

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.text:
State on 22 November 2026: NONE DEPLOYED OR PAID FOR BY THIS PR.
The infrastructure under infra/azure and the manual workflow .github/workflows/p3-azure-review-deploy.yml are a reviewable deployment route for the actual FleetFlow API. This is not proof of a live Azure deployment. The hosted frontend continues to be separate. GitHub-hosted runners cannot serve as private network peers to a database or event broker.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Decisions before applying anything
chunks.text: 1. Budget and subscription: identify Azure subscription, region, quotas and a monthly spending cap with alert notifications. Confirm cost of Storage, Log Analytics, Container Apps, private endpoints, PostGIS and Kafka. Container Apps may include a monthly free grant but the entire architecture is not free and quotas may change. No work is allowed to claim all components fit a zero-cost tier. 2. Sensitive data: synthetic GPS only for portfolio testing. Determine retention, privacy, access controls and region before real telemetry. 3. External data plane: prepare an accessible, secured PostgreSQL database with PostGIS and reviewed schema migrations, plus a real TLS-enabled Kafka-compatible broker. Neither is created by this minimal Terraform module. Private ingress defaults to false and the app will not be reachable from the public internet. 4. Actual API image: build, vulnerability-scan and publish the backend/Dockerfile image to a registry the Azure Container App can read, pinned to an immutable digest. If using a private registry, add reviewed managed-identity pull access; the example does not implement registry authentication. 5.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Decisions before applying anything
chunks.text: Environment security: configure GitHub environment azure-review with a required human approval rule. Add branch restrictions and audit trail. Do not assume the workflow automatically configures those rules. 6. Identity: create an Azure workload-identity federation to GitHub Actions, restricted to this repository's azure-review environment, with least-privilege resource-group access, not tenant-wide admin. 7. Terraform state: bootstrap a separate Azure Blob state storage account and container with Azure AD RBAC, encryption, access restrictions, logging, retention and state locking. The application lake storage account is different from the preexisting state store. No local runner Terraform state for an actual deployment. 8. Runtime readiness: add a real public health/reachability route through an approved ingress path or internal probe, verify DNS/TLS, CORS, auth, restart/replay, backup/restore, alerts, costs and teardown.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Required GitHub configuration
chunks.text:
Repository-level variables, available to the preflight guard:
- AZURE_TFSTATE_RG: existing state storage resource group - AZURE_TFSTATE_ACCOUNT: existing state account name - AZURE_TFSTATE_CONTAINER: existing Blob state container - AZURE_FLEETFLOW_STORAGE_NAME: globally unique application lake account - AZURE_FLEETFLOW_API_IMAGE: immutable reviewed image reference (when enabling API) - AZURE_FLEETFLOW_KAFKA_SERVERS: TLS/private broker address (when enabling API) - AZURE_FLEETFLOW_BUDGET_REVIEWED: set true only after real budget review
Environment secrets, under the protected azure-review environment:
- AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID - FLEETFLOW_DATABASE_URL (only for actual API deployment) - FLEETFLOW_JWT_SECRET_KEY (only for actual API deployment, at least 32 chars)
The GitHub OIDC identity requires appropriate Azure control-plane RBAC and Blob Data Contributor access to the separate state container. Terraform sensitive values can appear in remote state; protect that state and rotate credentials. Do not enter secrets in issues, PRs or .tfvars files.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Manual flow
chunks.text:
The workflow dispatch action becomes discoverable when the workflow exists on the repository default branch after reviewed merge. Select a reviewed ref. Run operation=plan first and inspect changes with the team. It uses OIDC and the remote state backend. No apply happens on plan.
Only after budget, security and environment approval, run operation=apply and enter the exact acknowledgement I_ACCEPT_AZURE_CHARGES. That job executes Terraform apply using the approved plan and existing state store. The workflow deliberately does not create the external PostGIS/Kafka services; deploy_api defaults false. If enabled, deploy and verify backend ingress and event replay separately.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Evidence required to mark Azure complete
chunks.text: Evidence required to mark Azure complete: Capture without sensitive values: subscription alias, repo commit, Terraform state revision, plan/apply run URLs, Azure resource IDs, digest of container actually running, health and real contract verification from an authorised network, log/metric alerts, measured cost and teardown/recreate proof. Azure code validated and Azure app deployed are different completion states. Never publish private endpoints, secrets or customer GPS.

chunks.title: Azure release execution gate — FleetFlow
chunks.heading: Teardown
chunks.text: Teardown: Only destroy resources in the dedicated Terraform state using a reviewed terraform plan -destroy, within an approved change and retention window. Ensure data/backups are preserved before deleting state or resources. Never destroy another project's group by name alone.

chunks.text: - Draft PR #12 disables both previously scheduled Airflow jobs (schedule_interval=None). chunks.title: FleetFlow — evidence-led engineering case study (November 2026)
chunks.heading: Design decisions and failure cases
chunks.text: 1. At-least-once events, not exactly-once claims. Outbox rows are committed with business state, then published with broker ACK. A crash between ACK and SQL update may replay; consumers reject old or duplicate events. Failed payloads have a durable quarantine path. 2. Unapproved is not deployed. The optimiser computes route candidates with constraints; a dispatcher must explicitly approve persisted plans. Distance and travel-time assumptions are illustrative without verified routing-network input. 3. Event time wins over delivery order. A newer valid GPS event is never rolled back by an older packet; reconnects use PostgreSQL snapshots. Disconnected or older-than-60-second observations are not labelled live. 4. Permissions apply to every path. Driver/depot/admin scopes are checked against current database identity on snapshots/broadcasts; anonymous REST endpoints must not reveal coordinates. Session expiry and revocation are not automatically a production-grade distributed authorization system. 5. Raw data is not the curated answer. Event IDs, UTC timestamps, allowed lateness, partition dates, row-count/average reconciliation and immutable SHA256 artifacts make local backfills inspectable. 6. Real tooling does not imply live production.

chunks.text: Review: draft PR #9, based on draft PR #8. Neither branch has been merged to main, publicly deployed or used to provision AWS.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — authenticated GPS stream and non-mocked full-stack proof
chunks.heading: Data-protection contract
chunks.text: - A browser sends an access JWT only as the first WebSocket frame {"action":"authenticate","token":"<access-token>"}, within five seconds. Never send a JWT in a URL, cookie or subprotocol. The server explicitly rejects refresh tokens, bad signatures, expired tokens, unknown/deactivated users, stale JWT roles, viewers and identities without explicit scope. - No implicit subscription exists. Only the vehicles channel is supported. A successful authenticated frame permits a subscribe request; a subscribed acknowledgement gates the browser's connected status. - A driver sees only vehicles currently assigned to their linked User.driver_id. A dispatcher sees vehicles in their explicitly assigned User.depot_id; NULL grants no access. An administrator may see the full local test fleet. An anonymous user or viewer has no GPS access. Scope is loaded from PostgreSQL, not trusted from JWT claims. - PostGIS snapshots on subscribe/reconnect are filtered by current scope. Every Kafka-to-WebSocket broadcast rechecks the DB identity, role, depot, driver assignment and access-token expiry. Revocation closes the socket.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — authenticated GPS stream and non-mocked full-stack proof
chunks.heading: Data-protection contract
chunks.text:
Message/snapshot fields do not embed credentials. - REST GET /api/v1/vehicles/{id}/location requires a signed-in, scoped user; unscoped vehicle/driver listings redact location fields. GPS write POST /api/v1/drivers/{id}/location rejects unlinked drivers and dispatchers without a matching depot. - New passwords are Argon2id, existing bcrypt hashes are verified through the supported bcrypt package. Refresh JWTs are accepted only at the explicit refresh endpoint. UTC login timestamps match the existing naive PostgreSQL timestamp column.
Privacy boundary: These protections are validated for a single-process local development topology. ENVIRONMENT!=development still disables WebSocket handshakes; this PR does not grant permission for public production streaming. Strong TLS termination, rate limiting, user/device revocation semantics, multi-instance broadcast fanout, historical retention controls, encryption/observability review and externally hosted deployment remain open gates.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — authenticated GPS stream and non-mocked full-stack proof
chunks.heading: Non-mocked acceptance
chunks.text:
CI file: .github/workflows/gps-full-stack.yml.
1. Provision disposable PostGIS and Redpanda containers on a hosted CI runner, with a guarded local fleetflow_test database. 2. Initialize the ORM schema and exercise additive migrations 03_dispatch_reliability.sql through 06_websocket_dispatch_scope.sql; no production database touched. 3. Generate temporary JWT signing secret and password in the runner; seed a synthetic depot, driver, vehicle, Argon2id user. No real driver location, customer records or external credentials. 4. Start FastAPI and the supervised local outbox worker. Wait for the GPS consumer's Kafka group assignment before publishing. 5. Open Chromium without routeWebSocket or HTTP intercepts. Log in via the real FastAPI endpoint; wait for authenticated GPS subscription. 6. Submit a real driver GPS update, assert the API says 202 queued; the outbox worker publishes to real Redpanda; the consumer commits a PostGIS coordinate and sends a scoped vehicle_update. Assert the browser displays the exact latitude/longitude, Kafka event source and fresh state. Independently query the scoped DB-backed REST endpoint. 7. Verify unauthenticated GPS REST returns 401; sign out and verify browser state is cleared.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.text: Review status: New draft implementation. This is local-first application code, not a live Kafka integration test or proof of a production service.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Reliability contract
chunks.text: 1. Dispatcher approves an already-persisted, validated planned route. 2. The same PostgreSQL transaction writes the approved route state, one route_approval_audit row (authenticated actor UUID, timestamp, status transition and event ID), and one pending dispatch_outbox row. 3. A separate worker selects due outbox rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes to the routes.approved topic and waits for a delivery ACK. Only confirmed deliveries are marked published; timeouts/NACKs remain pending with bounded exponential backoff. 4. The RouteEventsConsumer validates the receipt against both the real approved route and matching audit row, then inserts an inbox receipt under unique (consumer_name, event_id). Its enclosing DB transaction commits after verification, before the Kafka offset is acknowledged. 5. A repeated event with the same ID has no second inbox side effect.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Reliability contract
chunks.text: This implements at-least-once delivery with transactional DB deduplication. A crash after Kafka ACK but before the DB's published commit may send the event again. The consumer must use event_id rather than assuming exactly once. External side effects such as WebSocket pushes are NOT atomically covered by the inbox receipt; do not call this end-to-end exactly-once delivery.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Database setup is explicit
chunks.text:
A new SQL file db/init/03_dispatch_reliability.sql adds the three tables, indexes, route approval status and database trigger protecting audit rows from UPDATE or DELETE. On a fresh database where db/init scripts are applied in sequence, it runs after 01_postgis_schema.sql. Existing databases must apply it explicitly, in a reviewed, approved maintenance window:
# EXAMPLE ONLY; adjust connection/permissions, no production run by ChatGPT psql "$DATABASE_URL_FOR_PSQL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -1 \ -f db/init/03_dispatch_reliability.sql
DATABASE_URL_FOR_PSQL must be a psql-compatible Postgres URI, not the asyncpg SQLAlchemy URL. No tables are dropped and no user records are copied. The script recreates the same audit trigger when re-applied.
The ORM test suite creates these tables via SQLAlchemy metadata in isolated fleetflow_test, but the append-only database trigger is supplied by the explicit SQL migration, not by create_all. The trigger regression test installs the identical trigger on its isolated test transaction and verifies UPDATE and DELETE fail. Test schema setup is not a production migration.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Run the worker (explicit opt-in)
chunks.text:
cd backend python -m pip install -e ".[dev,lake]" # Set a configured PostgreSQL URL and Kafka brokers in the environment. python -m src.reliability.worker --once # Only under process supervision + alerting: python -m src.reliability.worker --forever --interval 2
There is no implicit publish daemon hidden inside FastAPI startup. A successful API response reports delivery_status=pending, not delivered. Worker process health, backlogs, dead letters, retention, telemetry and resilience at sustained load need further verification.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Independent acceptance tests
chunks.text:
cd backend # CI uses only local PostGIS fleetflow_test with JWT_SECRET_KEY set. pytest tests/test_api/test_dispatch_reliability.py -v pytest tests/test_unit/test_outbox_ack.py -v pytest --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing -v ruff check src/ black --check src/
Test assertions cover:
- One audit row + one pending event from one role-gated approval. - A repeated approval returns a conflict and does not add another event. - A simulated Kafka timeout leaves the event pending and schedules retry. - A later simulated ACK publishes that same event ID. - Inbox deduplication of redelivered IDs, and rollback on handler failure. - Real Postgres trigger rejects UPDATE and DELETE on approval audit rows. - A fake Kafka producer's ACK/NACK/timeout callbacks, not an actual broker.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — approval audit, transactional outbox and inbox
chunks.heading: Intentional limits and next step
chunks.text: Intentional limits and next step: Not yet evidenced: broker-backed restart/replay with actual Kafka, a transactional outbox for all other route/order events, duplicate-safe WebSocket notification, DLQ/poison-event policy, operational backlog alarms, 24-hour event-time corner cases, deployed AWS/Vercel backend and full source→Kafka→dispatch→GPS→analytics demo. No AWS resources were provisioned.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.text: Review status: stacked draft PR #8 on PR #7; code CI and separate browser tests verified on commit c27af41f38b4a14f535372465206249481d1a54d. This integration is deliberately local-development only. Public hosted telemetry is disabled until a permission-scoped, authenticated WebSocket handshake and reviewed deployment model exist. Do not call a Vercel build a live backend deployment.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.heading: What is real
chunks.text: 1. An authenticated driver with a linked User.driver_id sends POST /api/v1/drivers/{driver_id}/location. Admin and dispatcher roles can submit for controlled local testing. Invalid/foreign credentials fail. 2. The API writes gps.location into the existing transactional PostgreSQL outbox; HTTP 202 queued means Kafka delivery is pending, not completed. No direct vehicle geolocation is falsely marked delivered. 3. Start the supervised outbox worker; it publishes using the real broker ACK and retries. The GPSLocationConsumer validates event_id, schema version 1, signed/offset-aware timestamp, finite geographic values and current vehicle/driver assignment. It updates the vehicle's PostGIS point, last_gps_at, last_gps_event_id and coordinates under row locking. It drops duplicate and older observed timestamps without broadcasting them. 4. The consumer uses the same in-process ConnectionManager as FastAPI's /ws endpoint, not a disconnected standalone process. 5. A local browser opens /tracking, subscribes to the vehicles channel and receives vehicle_update. On connection or reconnection, the server supplies up to 100 actual last-known vehicle positions from PostGIS in vehicle_snapshot. 6.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.heading: What is real
chunks.text: Frontend validates UUIDs, coordinate ranges, timestamps and event time, never rewinds positions on delayed/snapshot updates, retries with capped exponential backoff and marks data stale after 60 seconds or offline when the socket is disconnected. A socket being connected is not itself proof of fresh telemetry.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.heading: Local-only boundaries and security
chunks.text: - Set ENVIRONMENT=development on the API only for trusted local work and use an Origin in WEBSOCKET_ALLOWED_ORIGINS, default localhost:3000/3001 or 127.0.0.1:3000. An arbitrary Origin is rejected; non-development WebSocket sessions are rejected. Browser clients cannot see positions without explicitly subscribing to vehicles. - The unauthenticated live WebSocket is not production-safe, even with an Origin check. Do not expose the development WebSocket service to the public internet. An authenticated socket handshake, per-role depot permissions, rate limiting and deployment isolation are release blockers. - The HTTP broadcast endpoint is disabled unless WEBSOCKET_BROADCAST_TOKEN is explicitly configured. The standalone WebSocket module no longer starts sample GPS broadcasts. Kafka and browser live updates run inside the shared FastAPI process, not in two separate in-memory servers. Multi-instance deployment needs Redis/NATS pubsub. - The public /demo still shows seeded demonstration vehicles/routes; it must not be represented as live. /tracking never generates a random sample vehicle.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.heading: Local-only boundaries and security
chunks.text: In hosted environments without NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_URL, the browser displays Not configured, never a fabricated LIVE badge. - GPS data collection should use consent and access controls in any real fleet. There is currently no driver-location history retention policy or multi-tenant isolation.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — local live GPS tracking console
chunks.heading: Reproducibility
chunks.text:
Apply additive migration db/init/05_gps_tracking.sql after 03 and 04 on an approved local database, or initialize a fresh PostGIS database from the repository's migration chain. Do not run against production without a reviewed migration plan.
Start local PostGIS, broker, backend and outbox worker in separate terminals. For example with environment correctly configured:
cd backend python -m pip install -e ".[dev,lake]" # Backend serves HTTP /api/v1 and WebSocket /ws on the same port. uvicorn src.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 # In another terminal: python -m src.reliability.worker --forever --interval 2 # Frontend (another terminal): cd ../frontend pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm dev # Visit http://localhost:3000/tracking
A dispatcher/driver JWT must be obtained from the existing login path. The authenticated GPS POST returns an event ID and delivery_status=pending. Once the outbox worker publishes it and the subscribed GPS consumer has committed the position, /tracking can show the fresh vehicle. Without the worker or Kafka, the tracking console will show no data or stale data.

chunks.heading: Acceptance evidence
chunks.text: - PostgreSQL tests cover driver identity enforcement, queued outbox without premature DB movement, actual PostGIS position update, duplicate and late event suppression, invalid GPS and mismatch rejection, WebSocket subscriptions/snapshots, and local Origin policy. - Browser Playwright tests intercept the WebSocket with controlled fixture packets to validate stale, reconnect, marker and no-fake-state UX. chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.text:
Status: implementation proposed in draft PR; CI and full-stack integration evidence must be checked on this branch head before this feature is called verified.
This milestone makes a narrow, real part of the dispatch golden path possible: PostGIS orders/customers + available driver/vehicle → real OR-Tools solver → persisted planned Route and RouteStop rows → existing dispatcher approval API.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.heading: Why the earlier path was misleading
chunks.text: Why the earlier path was misleading: Previously, POST /api/v1/optimization/routes/optimize could import a solver from an uninstalled repository-level ml package. The optimiser expected latitude and longitude on Order, although the actual ORM has them on Customer. It also only returned transient route proposals. The new packaged solver lives in backend/src/optimization/route_optimizer.py; historical ML smoke imports use a thin compatibility wrapper, preventing separate solver implementations.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.heading: Explicit operations
chunks.text:
All requests require a running local backend, isolated PostGIS with seed data, and the environment's appropriate authentication configuration.
1. Preview (read-only): POST /api/v1/optimization/routes/optimize. 2. Save proposals (dispatcher/admin token): POST /api/v1/optimization/routes/plan. 3. Inspect the created route IDs using GET /api/v1/routes/{route_id}. 4. Approve with POST /api/v1/routes/{route_id}/approve as dispatcher/admin. 5. Only an approved route may be started by an authorised assigned driver.
JSON input for preview and plan:
{"depot_id": "REPLACE_WITH_SEEDED_DEPOT_UUID", "date": "2030-01-15"}
Plan creation is not approval, dispatch activation, route acceptance by a real driver, or proof that GPS reaches the map. The plan endpoint holds row locks, rejects overlapping active route/order assignments and commits all Route/Stop rows together. The same order may not be silently planned twice while an active plan exists. Historical/cancelled routes have separate lifecycle semantics.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.heading: Data and solver constraints
chunks.text: - Customers supply actual demo-seed geocoordinates. Missing locations are rejected instead of silently substituting a zero-distance stop. - Drivers must be assigned to available vehicles. Eligible orders must be pending at the selected depot and delivery date. - Per-vehicle capacity is modelled in grams to avoid truncating fractional kilograms. The depot and order windows must fit one UTC route date. - Route distance is a Haversine straight-line approximation, not road mileage. Illustrative travel time assumes 30 km/h. UI and README must not label these results as real-world observed distances or ETAs. - OR-Tools returns feasible candidates under its encoded capacity and time constraints, not proven globally optimal routes. - Before persistence, the API checks stop sequence, order coverage, driver, capacity and arrival windows. Approval is a separate API operation. - Complete driver duty-hour constraints, live traffic, road restrictions and fuel/CO₂ optimisation are not implemented here.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.heading: Acceptance test and checks
chunks.text:
cd backend python -m pip install -e ".[dev,lake]" # Isolated local PostGIS test database, never production: export DATABASE_URL="postgresql+asyncpg://fleetflow:fleetpass@localhost:5432/fleetflow_test" # Provide a securely generated ephemeral JWT_SECRET_KEY in the test environment. pytest tests/test_api/test_dispatch_planning.py -v pytest --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing -v ruff check src/ black --check src/ cd .. python -m pytest ml/tests/test_core_ml_smoke.py -q
GitHub Actions additionally runs frontend lint/types/build and high/critical dependency scanning. The acceptance cases cover read-only preview, solver location correctness, persistence, explicit approval boundary, duplicate-plan rejection, authorisation, unavailable vehicle, missing location and infeasible capacity. Test evidence should be linked to the exact matching head SHA.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P1 — Optimiser-generated planned dispatch
chunks.heading: Still not a complete end-to-end system
chunks.text:
Kafka ingestion remains separate from this API transaction. There is no durable transactional outbox or inbox, no actual Kafka-to-WebSocket browser smoke test, and no reconciled dispatch mart or production cloud deployment. This is a local-first milestone. No AWS resources are provisioned.
Next: immutable approval audit event, event outbox/inbox with replay tests, driver/vehicle duty-hour validation, live UI telemetry and analytical reconciliation, each with independent acceptance evidence.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.text: Status: REVIEW BRANCH / NOT DEPLOYED. All GPS data below must be synthetic. This addition does not merge the upstream draft stack or change the hosted demo.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: Architectural boundary
chunks.text:
Synthetic authenticated GPS -> existing Kafka/PostGIS -> accepted JSONL snapshot -> existing replay validation/quarantine -> immutable clean Parquet
+-> existing Postgres hourly load -> dbt GPS fact + observed dimensions | +-> real PySpark aggregate -> optional Databricks Delta managed table
Azure review-only Terraform -> private ADLS Gen2 storage foundation -> optional gated Container App for an externally supplied backend image, PostGIS and broker
Important: The Databricks Free Edition workspace is independent of the user's Azure subscription. Provisioning an Azure Storage account does not connect it to Databricks or imply that the notebook has accessed Azure data. The hosted FleetFlow site remains a fixture-backed portfolio frontend unless a real backend deployment is independently verified.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 1. Build a source snapshot (local)
chunks.text:
From the repository root with dependencies installed:
python -m pip install -e './backend[lake]' PYTHONPATH=backend python -m src.lakehouse.replay \ --input /absolute/path/to/synthetic-gps.jsonl --output /tmp/fleetflow-lake
The command reports the content-addressed directory /tmp/fleetflow-lake/runs/<run_key>/. Inspect manifest.json and validate each listed checksum before importing data anywhere else. Accepted GPS Parquet lives under clean/event_date=*/telemetry.parquet (or clean/empty.parquet). Never upload real vehicle/person locations to a free demonstration account.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 2. Rebuild the batch aggregation in actual local Spark
chunks.text:
python -m pip install 'pyspark==3.5.6' 'pytest==8.3.5' PYTHONPATH=data-engineering/spark SPARK_LOCAL_HOSTNAME=localhost \ python -m pytest -q data-engineering/spark/test_fleetflow_batch.py
The Spark module reads accepted replay Parquet, groups by observed vehicle and UTC hour, counts accepted/late records, computes mean observed speed and selects a deterministic most-recent coordinate. It rejects duplicate IDs and out-of-contract records. It does not stream Kafka, provision a Spark cluster, infer drive distance, or forecast ETA. The existing Python replay remains the raw-event contract and quarantine authority.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 3. Run in Databricks Free Edition
chunks.text: 1. Create a Free Edition workspace using the official Azure Databricks signup route. Do not start a paid Azure Databricks workspace just for this exercise. 2. Import the repository as a Git folder. Open data-engineering/spark/fleetflow_databricks.py as a notebook with the sibling fleetflow_batch.py present. 3. Upload the entire original run directory (manifest, raw, clean, quarantine) into a Unity Catalog Volume you control (for example /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/<run_key>/). 4. Fill widget parameters: manifest_path pointing at the uploaded JSON and, only when publishing, output_table in catalog.schema.table form. The notebook discovers exact clean files from the manifest, verifies the SHA-256 for every artifact, and reconciles Spark event/late counts before writing. 5. Run in preview mode first. Review displayed rows and original run counts. Set publish=yes only for a new, dedicated Delta table. The notebook refuses to overwrite a pre-existing table. 6. Record a screenshot of the successful Spark execution, SQL count query, Delta table path, workspace/runtime version, cost/usage quota and execution date in the evidence register. Do not claim Databricks until this executes.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 3. Run in Databricks Free Edition
chunks.text:
The manifest checks establish byte integrity against the supplied manifest, not the authenticity of whoever authored that manifest. Keep the run synthetic.
The notebook does not create an Azure storage credential, production table or external integration. Free Edition quotas and feature availability can change.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 4. dbt star model on the existing PostgreSQL warehouse
chunks.text: The star now contains: Model · Grain / join key · Measure or intentfct_gps_hourly · one replay + vehicle + UTC hour, gps_hour_key · observed event count, late count, measured speed dim_observed_vehicle · one replay + vehicle, vehicle_run_key · first/last observed hours, not fleet inventory dim_utc_date · one observed UTC calendar day, utc_date_key · calendar attributes only Both dimension keys are linked to the fact through schema relationship tests. A singular SQL test rejects impossible late counts and out-of-hour latest positions. The existing actual local PostGIS/dbt CI must pass on this branch before marking warehouse coverage verified. This does not fabricate order delivery KPIs or driver availability.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 5. Terraform: Azure review infrastructure, not an executed deployment
chunks.text:
infra/azure/ provisions a resource group and private, HTTPS-only hierarchical storage foundation. A Container App, its environment and Log Analytics are disabled by default via deploy_api=false. The opt-in API depends on an actual published backend container image plus reachable PostGIS and Kafka, none of which are automatically created by this module.
Static review only (no Azure credentials or billable resources needed):
terraform -chdir=infra/azure fmt -check -recursive terraform -chdir=infra/azure init -backend=false terraform -chdir=infra/azure validate
For a later approved cloud deployment, first establish budget/credit, subscription quota, suitable region, secured remote state, least-privilege identity/RBAC, non-public network connectivity, real database+broker, container registry access, image provenance, health/recovery checks and a teardown plan. Then authenticate with az login, choose the subscription, provide a unique storage name and inspect terraform plan. Never run terraform apply by default. Resources and observability can incur charges even where a service has a monthly free allowance. Strong secrets passed to Terraform can be stored in state; keep it encrypted and access-controlled.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 5. Terraform: Azure review infrastructure, not an executed deployment
chunks.text: With public ingress disabled, the optional API Container App has no public endpoint. Enabling public ingress without completing the authz, TLS/domain, rate-limit, monitoring and integration review is not a production release.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: 6. Optional Snowflake experiment
chunks.text: Do not claim Snowflake until a separate free-trial workspace actually executes a translated version of the observed GPS star model and its relationship / freshness checks. These models currently use PostgreSQL-specific SQL casts, TO_CHAR and intervals; they are not portable to Snowflake merely by changing a dbt profile. A Snowflake trial is optional, not a dependency of the FleetFlow core golden path.

chunks.title: FleetFlow / Spark + Databricks + dbt + optional Azure
chunks.heading: Release gate
chunks.text: Release gate: P0/P1 upstream issues, 24/7 operational reliability, real Azure / Databricks execution, cloud cost measurement, security and approved draft-stack merge remain separate work. Add dated CI run URLs, exact commit and workspace proof to docs/EVIDENCE_REGISTER.md once verified. Until then, label every new integration as code committed / CI pending / cloud not executed.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.text: Draft PR #12, stacked on draft PR #11.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: What changed, and why
chunks.text:
Before this review, the old daily_route_optimization Airflow DAG contained a hard-coded NYC depot, called an obsolete optimization API path, and wrote route/stop rows directly without a dispatcher approval. The old hourly_demand_forecast DAG synthesized demand 5 when missing and advertised an uncalibrated 0.8 confidence, with invented driver-positioning guidance. Both were enabled on fixed automatic schedules.
Both are now schedule_interval=None (manual-only), catchup=False, and max_active_runs=1. The dispatch DAG runs only read-only, aggregate SQL after receiving an explicit date and a configured synchronous PostgreSQL connection. The forecasting DAG requires an operator-provided, validated hourly CSV; it does not insert routes, send driver instructions, or serve guessed confidence. Every actual route plan remains in the authenticated FastAPI plan/approve workflow.
The optional Airflow 2.8.2 Docker dev profile now uses SequentialExecutor, compatible with its local SQLite metadata database. It mounts backend and dags read-only, binds the UI to localhost and uses an ignored local input directory. This profile remains development only, not a production HA scheduler.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: Baseline contract
chunks.text:
backend/src/analytics/forecast_baselines.py validates a strict UTC hourly sequence with zero missing/duplicate/unordered hours and nonnegative integer counts. It accepts a CSV with exactly timestamp_utc,count, or creates a deterministic synthetic 12-week fixture with seed 42. Input rows never contain customer, vehicle or employee identities.
The evaluation uses the last 168 hours as a chronological holdout and an expanding one-hour-ahead walk-forward protocol: each prediction uses actual observations strictly before its target time. Four naive baselines (last-hour, same hour yesterday, same hour last week, trailing 24-hour mean) are compared using MAE, RMSE and WAPE. WAPE is null when the entire test period has zero demand (rather than inventing 100% accuracy). There is no random-split leakage or "ML superiority" claim.
This is not Prophet/XGBoost/LSTM training, future 24-hour multi-step model validation or evidence of accuracy on real orders. It is the minimum reproducible control benchmark those models must beat on a future real-life, privacy-reviewed chronological dataset.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: Reproduce the synthetic baseline
chunks.text:
python -m pip install -e './backend[dev]' python -m pytest backend/tests/test_analytics/test_forecast_baselines.py -v python -m src.analytics.forecast_baselines \ --weeks 12 --seed 42 --holdout-hours 168 \ --output /tmp/fleetflow-synthetic-forecast-results.json python -m json.tool /tmp/fleetflow-synthetic-forecast-results.json
For an explicitly supplied hourly anonymous count CSV:
python -m src.analytics.forecast_baselines \ --input /path/to/hourly_counts.csv --holdout-hours 168 \ --output /tmp/fleetflow-validated-baselines.json
Any missing hour, duplicate, naive timezone or additional PII column makes the input validation fail rather than silently filling it.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: Local manual Airflow usage
chunks.text:
The data Compose profile is optional. After manually reviewing .env and Docker credentials, put a non-sensitive hourly CSV in data-engineering/airflow/input/ (this folder is gitignored). Configure FLEETFLOW_HOURLY_COUNTS_CSV to the container path /opt/fleetflow/input/YOUR_FILE.csv. For dispatch readiness, set FLEETFLOW_ANALYTICS_DATABASE_URL to a synchronous PostgreSQL URL with SELECT-only permissions; the task also uses SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY. No file or SQL result should contain a driver's GPS coordinates or customer address.
Run the Airflow profile manually, open the loopback-only UI, and trigger daily_route_optimization with {"route_date":"2030-01-15"}, or hourly_demand_forecast with an explicitly supplied source path. This is a manual evaluation. There is no ongoing daily dispatch, actual automatic ETA pipeline, or production cron in this PR.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: CI and evidence
chunks.text: - Forecast/Airflow CI 44110285107 at code SHA c037568a99d916f1eb3c8490a80e23a69caea49a: 6 chronological/negative tests passed; four synthetic baseline predictions were evaluated; official Airflow 2.8.2 DAGBag import passed with both manual-only DAGs and zero import errors. Earlier Airflow parsing correctly caught datetime.UTC unavailable on its Python 3.8 image, repaired to timezone.utc. - Synthetic fixed-seed, one-step 168h holdout: last_hour MAE 3.7857, last_day 2.5774, last_week 2.1250, trailing_day_mean 5.1863 (units: synthetic orders/hour, not production accuracy). - Python 3.11 Ruff requires a documented exception for the Python 3.8-compatible timezone.utc spelling. Later code/Compose/docs commits require matching exact-head CI before calling PR #12 green.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — chronological demand baselines and manual-only Airflow
chunks.heading: Outstanding P2/P3/P4
chunks.text: No production Airflow scheduling or event-time warehouse backfill, automatic Kafka → Parquet capture, performance SLA or data retention policy. Routes still use approximate fixed-speed Haversine. Real holdout datasets, multi-step forecasting, actual route impacts, Terraform plan/validate, AWS budget and IAM sign-off, cloud teardown, full system cost and public portfolio case study are separate gates. Neither the optional Airflow profile nor the synthetic baselines has been deployed to real operations.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.text: Review: draft PR #10, stacked on draft PR #9. No main merge, AWS resources, public historical GPS feed or paid service.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.heading: Actual lineage
chunks.text:
Synthetic or exported GPS JSONL (bounded, offline) -> immutable raw/events.jsonl and source SHA-256 -> Pydantic GPS v1 validation, source-order watermark, dedupe/quarantine -> clean/event_date=YYYY-MM-DD/*.parquet (UTC event time + late flag) -> curated/hourly_vehicle_telemetry.parquet -> independent quality.py reconciliation and artifact audit
This is not a live Kafka-to-S3 pipeline: live Kafka-to-PostGIS-to-WebSocket was independently established in P1 GPS acceptance. The Parquet replay currently reads an explicitly supplied JSONL file.
PostGIS transactional orders, drivers, routes (current state) -> dbt PostgreSQL staging views (privacy-reduced driver rows) -> dbt Postgres daily KPI fact + driver-performance dimension -> 26 dbt schema/relationship-style/singular SQL quality checks -> deterministic synthetic fixture assertions
The dbt models are not derived from the Parquet telemetry, and should not be described as such. Current-state order and route tables are not a historical event log; rebuilding the dbt marts makes snapshot aggregates, not immutable as-of-date history.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.heading: Semantics and privacy
chunks.text: - Route statuses include planned (not approved), approved, in_progress, completed, cancelled. - Actual distance/duration and observed-vs-planned comparisons stay NULL when absent. A zero completed count is a legitimate zero; unobserved performance is not a legitimate 0% or 100% score. - Only completed routes with both an actual and a positive planned distance are compared for distance ratio. Do not mix all planned routes into this denominator. - dbt driver staging/marts intentionally omit name, email, phone and address. The raw transactional database still contains sensitive fields and must be access-controlled independently. Do not publish exported GPS files. - Late GPS events within the immutable replay are retained and marked; they are not silently discarded. Duplicate event IDs with conflicting payloads are quarantined. Cross-layer validation independently checks hourly counts, last coordinates, average speed, late counts, partition dates, source-row arithmetic, content hashes and missing/extra rows. - The fixture data in data-engineering/dbt/ci/seed_postgis.sql and backend/tests/fixtures/demo_gps_events.jsonl is deterministic, synthetic, and not actual fleet/customer performance.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.heading: Reproduce locally (only a disposable test database)
chunks.text:
Prerequisites: Python 3.11, a local disposable PostgreSQL 15 + PostGIS database named fleetflow_test with user fleetflow, and the dependencies below. Never run the CI fixture SQL against operational data.
python -m pip install -e './backend[dev,lake]' python -m pip install 'dbt-postgres>=1.9,<2'
export POSTGRES_HOST=localhost export POSTGRES_PORT=5432 export POSTGRES_USER=fleetflow export POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<your local test password>' export POSTGRES_DB=fleetflow_test export JWT_SECRET_KEY='<locally generated 32+ character test key>' export DBT_HOST=localhost export DBT_PORT=5432 export DBT_USER=fleetflow export DBT_PASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" export DBT_DATABASE=fleetflow_test export DBT_SCHEMA=public
python data-engineering/dbt/ci/bootstrap_test_db.py PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql -h localhost -U fleetflow -d fleetflow_test \
The last two commands are separate: replay prints the content-addressed run directory, then quality audits that exact directory. Do not literally enter <run-key>; substitute the printed value.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.heading: Verified inspectable CI
chunks.text: Code SHA 7d00451821f42cd198e16d5d87ae7ccb6f5a374e: Analytics run 44105602510 passed both jobs: - Real PostGIS + dbt 5 models, 26 data tests, 31 successful tasks (PASS=31 WARN=0 ERROR=0) and exact synthetic KPI SQL assertion. - Real PyArrow 12 replay tests + 6 quality tests passed. - CI preserves manifest.json and run_results.json as workflow artifacts. Earlier fixture-setup failures revealed required driver hours and order source fields; both are now explicitly seeded. The dbt run demonstrates model execution, not S3/Athena or a production dashboard.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reconciled analytics on two explicitly separate source paths
chunks.heading: Still missing (do not score as complete)
chunks.text: - Continuously replicated source to raw lake (currently manual batch replay). - Incremental tracked ingestion and point-in-time historical snapshots; no CDC/incremental dbt model is yet verified. - An actually executed Airflow scheduling run, retries/backfill operations, warehouse freshness alerting, data lineage artifacts for the full real dispatch event chain, provider outage tests. - Held-out routing and demand/ETA baseline evaluation with measured, timestamped costs and accuracy, p95 latency and cloud cost analysis. - Terraform plan/validate, human-approved optional AWS deployment/teardown, production privacy/retention and authenticated multi-worker socket fanout.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reproducible synthetic route-planning baseline evaluation
chunks.text: Draft PR #11 stacks on draft PR #10.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reproducible synthetic route-planning baseline evaluation
chunks.heading: Question
chunks.text:
On the same deliberately small synthetic logistics fixtures, how does real OR-Tools CVRPTW differ from two simple but capacity- and time-window-aware baselines?
The evaluators are input-order assignment and nearest feasible neighbour. All three methods are independently checked for weight capacity, service time, UTC windows, depot return and unassigned orders. No algorithm gets credit for short distance by dropping an order.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reproducible synthetic route-planning baseline evaluation
chunks.heading: Fixtures and limitations
chunks.text:
backend/src/optimization/heuristic_baselines.py specifies fixed synthetic vehicle IDs, depot/driver IDs, customer coordinates and order windows for city_feasible, window_feasible and capacity_infeasible. This is not a model training/held-out-accuracy experiment: a routing solver is not trained on these orders. No addresses are real.
The comparison uses rounded Haversine straight-line metres with a constant illustrative 30 km/h speed. Service time is five minutes per stop and all windows fall on a fixed UTC route date. This is not a road-network, live traffic, fuel or ETA benchmark.
An illustrative planning-cost sensitivity calculation is explicitly £0.35/km + £12/hour. These values are chosen assumptions, not actual employee wages, fuel costs, verified operating expenses or savings. Cost is null whenever a route set has unassigned orders or violates a constraint. Optimizer solve times are measured inside each CI runner and are machine-specific; compare with those caveats.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reproducible synthetic route-planning baseline evaluation
chunks.heading: Fixtures and limitations
chunks.text:
An illustrative planning-cost sensitivity calculation is explicitly £0.35/km + £12/hour. These values are chosen assumptions, not actual employee wages, fuel costs, verified operating expenses or savings. Cost is null whenever a route set has unassigned orders or violates a constraint. Optimizer solve times are measured inside each CI runner and are machine-specific; compare with those caveats.
Input-order and nearest-neighbour baseline schedules depart at the depot's fixed opening time; the OR-Tools planner may choose another feasible start within the same window. The reported aggregate scheduled duration includes waiting, not just driving. Objective comparison should primarily evaluate service coverage, feasibility and distance and should not treat illustrative cost as an economic win.

chunks.title: FleetFlow P2 — reproducible synthetic route-planning baseline evaluation
chunks.heading: Reproduction
chunks.text: Reproduction: python -m pip install -e './backend[dev]' python -m pytest backend/tests/test_optimization/test_heuristic_baselines.py -q python -m src.optimization.heuristic_baselines \ --solver-seconds 1 \ --output /tmp/fleetflow-route-baseline.json python -m json.tool /tmp/fleetflow-route-baseline.json For every scenario/method the output includes served, orders, unassigned, constraint_violations, total_distance_km, total_duration_minutes, solve_time_ms, illustrative_cost_gbp and is_feasible. CI stores the JSON as a downloadable workflow artifact, and prints each per-scenario result in job logs.

chunks.title: P2 routing benchmark — real OR-Tools versus capacity/window-aware baseline
chunks.text: New on a separate review branch; exact-head CI must pass before claiming verification. The benchmark uses the existing VehicleRoutingOptimizer with real OR-Tools, not simulated routes, compared to a deterministic first-feasible nearest-neighbour planner on the same original synthetic depot, customer positions, vehicle capacities, 4-minute service times and UTC delivery windows. Three fixed fixtures include eight stops/one van, twelve stops/two vans, and an intentionally impossible capacity case. Each method is evaluated independently for assignment count, missing stops, time-window/capacity/duplicate violations, straight-line Haversine kilometres, summed route durations, one-run solver execution milliseconds and illustrative GBP cost at 0.35 per kilometre. If one method leaves more stops unassigned, its distance/cost must not be compared as a savings estimate.

chunks.title: P2 routing benchmark — real OR-Tools versus capacity/window-aware baseline
chunks.text:
The optimiser uses straight-line distance and a fixed 30 km/h speed; neither is a verified road-network ETA. Route duration is the planner's internal schedule estimate; no worker wages, fuel consumption, carbon, congestion, demand distribution or customer-facing SLA was measured. The nearest-neighbour planner respects constraints but deliberately performs no backtracking or vehicle reassignment. The infeasible case is explicitly reported as unassigned. A single successful synthetic run cannot establish superiority or production cost savings.
Reproduce from repository root: cd backend && PYTHONPATH=. python -m src.optimization.benchmark --output /tmp/fleetflow-routes.json. CI also uses PYTHONPATH=backend python -m pytest tests/test_routing_benchmark.py and uploads the exact benchmark JSON. The baseline, inputs, measured results and known limitations are independently reviewable. No paid provider, AWS resource, real GPS journey or production dispatch is invoked by this benchmark.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.text:
Status: Local batch replay implementation. Not connected to live Kafka, AWS, a production fleet, or a completed dispatch workflow.
This slice demonstrates an actual raw → validated → curated data journey for historical vehicle telemetry. It uses intentionally synthetic Glasgow-area coordinates with made-up IDs; no customer or driver records are represented as genuine.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Reproduce locally
chunks.text:
Requires Python 3.11+ and network access to install dependencies:
~~~bash cd backend python -m pip install -e ".[dev,lake]" python -m src.lakehouse.replay \ --input tests/fixtures/demo_gps_events.jsonl \ --output /tmp/fleetflow-lake \ --lateness-minutes 15 python -m pytest tests/test_lakehouse/test_replay.py -v ~~~
All replay runs are immutable and addressed by a digest of the input bytes and the lateness configuration. Re-running the same fixture should return the existing snapshot, rather than overwrite history.
The CLI prints the exact output directory, source SHA-256 and reconciliation counts. It also records SHA-256 checksums for each artifact, and refuses to reuse a snapshot if any artifact changes.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Data contract and provenance
chunks.text: Data contract and provenance: Input is newline-delimited JSON containing the existing FleetFlow GPSLocationEvent v1 contract (event_id, schema_version=1, timestamp with timezone, driver/vehicle UUIDs, coordinates, optional speed). Input event_id, timestamp, schema_version and event_type are required explicitly at the replay boundary (even though producers can generate defaults). Event timestamps are normalised to UTC; schema version, event type, coordinates and timestamps are validated.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Data contract and provenance > Actual output layout
chunks.text:
~~~text /tmp/fleetflow-lake/runs/<run-key>/ ├── manifest.json ├── raw/ │ └── events.jsonl # exact input bytes ├── clean/ │ └── event_date=YYYY-MM-DD/ │ └── telemetry.parquet # validated, deduplicated events ├── curated/ │ └── hourly_vehicle_telemetry.parquet # event counts and speed summaries └── quarantine/ └── rejected.jsonl # line and diagnostic, not copied payload ~~~
Clean layer: Parquet stores UUIDs, UTC timestamps, version, geolocation, speed, a late-event flag and the original input line for traceability. Each event ID appears at most once within a snapshot.
Curated layer: One row per vehicle per UTC hour with event count, late count, average reported speed and most recent event position. The most recent event is selected by event time, not arrival order.
Quarantine: Invalid JSON, wrong event type/version, missing or naive timestamps and bad coordinates are rejected with limited diagnostic information. Repeated identical event IDs count as duplicates; the same event ID with a conflicting payload goes to quarantine instead of quietly overriding earlier state.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Data contract and provenance > Actual output layout
chunks.text:
Quarantine: Invalid JSON, wrong event type/version, missing or naive timestamps and bad coordinates are rejected with limited diagnostic information. Repeated identical event IDs count as duplicates; the same event ID with a conflicting payload goes to quarantine instead of quietly overriding earlier state.
Late events: Arrival-order watermark is tracked per vehicle. Events older than the highest previously observed event-time by more than the configured lateness threshold are flagged, but retained in historical analytics. This demonstrates replay/backfill semantics, not a complete streaming watermark implementation.
Manifest: Source digest, run key, contract identifier, lateness threshold, artifact paths and reconciliation totals are generated without invented performance claims or wall-clock-dependent metadata.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Acceptance tests
chunks.text: The automated tests check: 1. A known event produces raw bytes, date-partitioned clean Parquet and a real curated Parquet table. 2. Two dates produce separate partitions; duplicates do not inflate KPI counts. 3. One deliberately late event is flagged and retained. 4. Conflicting IDs, invalid geolocation, unsupported schema versions and missing timezone information are rejected. 5. A repeated replay is immutable; changed input or lateness configuration produces a new run. 6. A fully invalid source still produces typed empty Parquet tables plus an inspectable quarantine. 7. Missing identity/time metadata is rejected, and tampered persisted files fail replay integrity checks.

chunks.title: FleetFlow — Reproducible Telemetry Lake Replay
chunks.heading: Known limitations and next engineering gate
chunks.text: - Batch-only: This script reads a local JSONL snapshot; no live Kafka subscription, incremental Kafka checkpoint or DLQ integration has been claimed. - No relational sink: It produces Parquet, not production PostgreSQL updates. - No object-storage deployment: The directory layout can be mapped to S3 later, but no AWS resources have been provisioned. - Single writer: Simultaneous writes to the same run key are not coordinated across processes. - Memory use: Accepted rows are currently held in memory. For very large datasets, stream to bounded Parquet row groups and use external-state deduplication. - PII: Store only permitted, non-sensitive and appropriately anonymised telemetry outside demo fixtures. - Data quality: Expand to contract registry, alertable quality metrics, reconciliation across live consumers and backfill policy. - Next golden path: Seed orders → ingest and validate events → persist route candidate → explicitly approve route → track GPS event → reconcile a curated dispatch-performance mart.

chunks.text: Career relevance: This demonstrates event-time correctness, schema validation, event identity and duplicates, partitioned Parquet, quarantine, replay and deterministic analytical calculations. It is evidence of a local data engineering prototype, not evidence of a professionally operated cloud production system.

chunks.title: FleetFlow ML evaluation — redesign branch
chunks.heading: What changed
chunks.text: - The forecasting module/package naming collision is fixed. - ML package exports load lazily, avoiding unrelated optional dependency imports. - Rolling features use past observations only. - Train/validation splits are chronological. - Feature and target scalers are fitted only on training samples per fold. - The LSTM restores the best validation epoch instead of the last epoch. - Model MAE is compared to a last-observation naive baseline in order counts. - Model weights have matching preprocessing metadata saved for inference.

chunks.title: FleetFlow ML evaluation — redesign branch
chunks.heading: Run
chunks.text: Run: Install the ML package's required Python dependencies in an isolated environment. python -m pytest ml/tests/test_forecasting_validation.py -q python -m ml.training.train_forecaster --epochs 10 --seed 42 Training defaults to generated synthetic hourly demand data. That is appropriate for software testing, not claims of real-world forecast accuracy. The training script writes fold reports under ml/training/metrics/ (or ML_METRICS_DIR) and model/preprocessing artifacts under ml/training/artifacts/.

chunks.title: FleetFlow ML evaluation — redesign branch
chunks.heading: Model acceptance gates
chunks.text: 1. Backtest on a versioned, timezone-normalized real demand dataset. 2. Report per-zone and per-hour MAE against seasonal naive baselines. 3. Use a final untouched time holdout after model selection. 4. Reject models that do not beat the baseline; never silently substitute synthetic predictions or invented confidence scores. 5. Deploy the approved model with version, training-data timestamp, inference latency, uncertainty interval and monitoring metadata. 6. Track model drift and data freshness before enabling dispatch recommendations.

chunks.title: FleetFlow README
chunks.heading: FLEETFLOW / THE DISPATCH ATLAS
chunks.text: FLEETFLOW / THE DISPATCH ATLAS: A city of constraints. A network of decisions. An engineering exploration of vehicle routing, event-driven logistics and operational visibility—from a depot's incoming orders to a route proposal a dispatcher can inspect. Explore the project · Dispatch decision sheet · Source evidence · Run locally These routes are hand-drawn conceptual geometry—not live GPS tracks, actual distances, or solver output.

chunks.title: FleetFlow README
chunks.heading: 01 / The dispatcher’s problem
chunks.text:
At the beginning of a delivery shift, a dispatcher has a moving puzzle: orders, stops, drivers, vehicle capacity, promised windows and the map between them.
An ordinary map shows where the trucks are. A dispatch system must also answer which jobs should go together, in what order, with what constraints—and what to do when circumstances change.
FleetFlow investigates both sides of that problem: a planning path for route optimization, and an observation path for locations and operational events.
The central idea: routing is a decision under constraints, not a decorative polyline.

That is not proof that the hosted site uses a live backend or that these unmerged changes are deployed. The event-processing module is explicitly filed under python_stream_processor, not Flink.

chunks.title: FleetFlow README
chunks.heading: The dispatch decision
chunks.text:
An architectural worksheet, not a screenshot or measured route. The preview endpoint remains read-only; the separately implemented plan endpoint persists unapproved routes, and dispatch requires explicit approval in stacked draft PRs.
The route engine has a concrete implementation path:
1. Choose a depot and date. Load the available vehicles and pending orders. 2. Apply constraints. Model capacity, depot location, route duration and service windows with OR-Tools. 3. Solve for a candidate. Compute and return routes when the dependencies and input data permit it. 4. Inspect before applying. The /optimize preview remains read-only; the explicit /plan path persists a planned route, and /approve is a separate, authorised dispatcher decision. These are demonstrated in stacked draft PRs, not deployed on the public site.
The optimizer uses an approximate distance/time calculation in the current source; OSRM has a separate optional local routing profile, not a verified dependency of every solver run. See route optimizer, optimization route and local-stack notes.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Real Avro and Schema Registry acceptance
chunks.text: Scope: synthetic test events → real Avro serializer → local Schema Registry → Kafka → GraphBuilder Avro decoder → SQLite source ledger → Neo4j graph. Not ML scoring, a live bank connection, or a deployed service.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Real Avro and Schema Registry acceptance
chunks.heading: Local run
chunks.text:
The disposable test environment uses localhost port 9092 for Kafka, 7687 for Neo4j, and 8082 for Schema Registry (the registry's container port is 8081).
python -m pip install -r requirements-ci.txt -r requirements-ingestion-ci.txt docker compose -f docker-compose.ingestion.yml up -d --wait GRAPHGUARD_INGESTION_INTEGRATION=1 pytest \ tests/integration/test_ingest_kafka_neo4j.py \ tests/integration/test_avro_registry.py -v docker compose -f docker-compose.ingestion.yml down --remove-orphans
