chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Real Avro and Schema Registry acceptance
chunks.heading: Verified only if tests pass
chunks.text: 1. The actual TransactionProducer serializes synthetic Pydantic events with the version-one Avro schema and obtains schema IDs from the live registry. 2. The registered subject is transactions.avro.acceptance-value. The produced record has Confluent's Avro magic byte and a non-zero schema ID, not a JSON fixture. 3. GraphBuilder resolves the schema ID through its real deserializer with JSON fallback disabled; writes a normalized source record first; then atomically applies its hash-checked graph projection. 4. A retry with the same transaction ID and normalized content does not add a duplicate transaction; different content under the same ID is quarantined through the existing acknowledged DLQ. 5. Replaying the same wire records with another consumer group leaves the first accepted source record and graph transaction unchanged. 6. A consumer configured with an unreachable registry URL refuses to advance the offset on an Avro decode fault. Reconnecting the same group to the correct URL enables it to replay and persist the event. 7. Naive datetime and nonfinite amounts are rejected by the producer model.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Real Avro and Schema Registry acceptance
chunks.heading: Verified only if tests pass
chunks.text:
The local ledger excludes source IP address and card fragments.
Failure-mode boundary: an unreachable URL simulates Schema Registry unavailability with real Avro/Kafka/Neo4j clients, but is not a chaos drill that stops the registry container. Version compatibility across evolving schemas and broker rebalance under concurrent partitions remain untested.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Real Avro and Schema Registry acceptance
chunks.heading: Contract boundaries
chunks.text: - The Avro schema defines schema_version=1. A new producer version needs compatibility testing and a documented migration. - Confluent wire-framed messages are never interpreted as JSON on failure. An unavailable registry or unreadable schema ID fails closed with the original Kafka offset available for replay; operators must investigate permanent poison Avro records to prevent a stuck consumer. - JSON is allowed only with GRAPHGUARD_JSON_FIXTURE_MODE=true for explicitly synthetic tests, not as a silent provider fallback. - The ledger is local SQLite/WAL for a reproducible demo. It is not a horizontally scalable, access-controlled system of record. Kafka commits occur after ledger and graph writes; a crash can replay a valid record. Do not advertise exactly-once processing. - No AWS account, paid service, cloud database or production data is used.

chunks.text:
Prerequisites: Python 3.11, Node.js 20, npm, and a clean checkout of the stacked PR #10 branch. Nothing requires AWS, paid APIs, actual customers or Docker for this quick UI fixture.
python -m pip install -r requirements-review-ci.txt npm --prefix frontend ci python -m ml.review.run_local_demo
Open http://127.0.0.1:3000/cases. The runner generates .local/graphguard-review/ on the first execution, including:
- models/manifest.json and deterministic 240-row synthetic baseline model artifacts, with independently pinned source/model hashes; - synthetic_ledger.sqlite3, containing three accepted synthetic ledger events with immutable pit-v1 snapshots; one case is opened with the real native SHAP explanation, and another transaction can be opened manually; - private_config.json and reviewer_tokens.json with file permissions 0600. chunks.text: Model state: experimental local research baseline, synthetic dataset only. Not approved to determine fraud, deny payments, accuse customers, or serve real financial data. This card covers the deterministic baseline evaluated in CI 43611311872, not an operational bank model. The generated model is loaded with an independently pinned artifact SHA-256 in PR #7.

chunks.title: GraphGuard synthetic research model card — pit-v1 (NOT production)
chunks.heading: Intended use and explicit exclusions
chunks.text:
Intended: demonstrate the engineering evidence chain from a first-observed synthetic ledger transaction through point-in-time features, a trained probability, model-derived SHAP and a human-only investigation workflow. Researchers can compare baselines and reproduce errors/latency locally.
Not intended: genuine fraud prediction; customer scoring, financial decisioning, payment approval/denial, debt/credit/lending eligibility, law-enforcement referral, regulatory audit, identity verification, discrimination/fairness assessment or large-scale deployment. SHAP is a model attribution, not a causal explanation or proof of wrongdoing. Review-close events are administrative case states, not fraud labels.

chunks.title: GraphGuard synthetic research model card — pit-v1 (NOT production)
chunks.heading: Algorithms and measured held-out results
chunks.text:
The experiment trains standardized, class-balanced logistic regression and weighted XGBoost with fixed parameters. It selects the model using validation PR-AUC, not test metrics; XGBoost was selected. An operating threshold was chosen to keep the validation-negative FPR at or below 5%, but this guarantee did not hold on untouched test data. Synthetic chronological holdout · Logistic regression · XGBoostPR-AUC / average precision · 0.6887 · 0.7650 ROC-AUC · 0.9072 · 0.9409 Precision@25 · 0.52 · 0.52 Recall at validation-selected threshold · 0.7500 · 0.8125 Realized test FPR · 6.25% · 9.375% Brier score · 0.0824 · 0.0695 Ten-bin ECE · 0.1120 · 0.0630 These figures are only for synthetic labels and a fixed generator, seed, split and dependency set. A better PR-AUC on the synthetic task does not establish operational superiority, accuracy on real bank data, demographic fairness, statistical significance or calibration.
Model artifacts SHA-256: logistic 35acf88762b6f54701f1d2453876b74b3fb9fca39b4dfa3d09d097d11235aece; XGBoost 87e40983a9294b60b3441c41f7c3c79ea1d0f7461d032cb6f429f1129a43a20e. These are artifact-integrity references, not cryptographic attestation of the developer or production model approval.

chunks.title: GraphGuard synthetic research model card — pit-v1 (NOT production)
chunks.heading: Validation-only post-calibration / drift research
chunks.text: P2_CALIBRATION_DRIFT.md describes an offline Platt-scaling experiment: calibration fitted on the held-out validation period, original untouched chronological test evaluated separately, 150 moving-block descriptive bootstrap resamples, and PSI for the 12 features and model score. Validation-period ECE is optimistic because it is in-sample calibration; PSI is not model concept drift or fairness proof. This model card does not claim live monitoring, deployed calibrated inference, automatic retraining, safe production thresholding or validated rollback.

chunks.title: GraphGuard synthetic research model card — pit-v1 (NOT production)
chunks.heading: Explainability and human review
chunks.text: The local verified SHAP implementation uses XGBoost native non-approximate TreeSHAP or exact linear Shapley attributions. Contributions are signed raw log odds and, with the baseline, reconstruct the same hash-verified model prediction. The local review API requires short-lived demo signer tokens for analyst/admin actions; the SQLite HMAC audit chain detects DB-only tampering without the separate signing key, but is not independently anchored or regulator-certified.

chunks.title: GraphGuard synthetic research model card — pit-v1 (NOT production)
chunks.heading: Known harms, limitations and mitigations
chunks.text: - Synthetic scoring mistakes and uncalibrated outputs must never trigger automatic decisions. The observed XGBoost 9.375% test FPR exceeds the nominal 5% target and is a concrete warning. - Historical proxies (shared devices, merchants, transaction volumes, amounts) may correlate with protected attributes or economic conditions. No protected-group data, subgroup metrics, fairness evaluation or human impact assessment is supplied; no claim of neutrality. - A narrow simulator can reward synthetic patterns not present in real-world fraud. Same-user and shared-device overlap may inflate apparent generalization; unseen-user and unseen-merchant stress tests are not complete. - Source hashes do not protect against an attacker holding all local signing keys and DB permissions. No enterprise identity, data retention policy, incident alerting, encryption-at-rest audit, independent log anchoring or multi-tenant isolation is demonstrated. - The legacy GAT, RAG and old hosted scoring API are not approved or interchangeable with this pit-v1 trained baseline.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — P2 offline calibration and shift monitor
chunks.text: Scope: research using original synthetic generator only. This report is not live and never changes the source ledger, case scores, persisted verdicts or hosted UI. python -m ml.monitoring.synthetic_calibration_drift --count 720 --seed 42 --output /tmp/graphguard-calibration.json trains the existing strict point-in-time Logistic/XGBoost baselines, selects the model using validation PR-AUC, fits Platt post-calibration using only the validation period, and compares raw and calibrated scores on the same untouched chronological test period. It selects respective 5% FPR target thresholds on validation negatives only. The observed test FPR may exceed 5%; the pipeline MUST report it rather than hiding or fixing the threshold based on test labels.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — P2 offline calibration and shift monitor
chunks.text: The JSON includes raw vs calibrated held-out PR-AUC, Brier, ECE, precision@K, operating FPR and recall; 150 fixed-seed moving-block descriptive PR-AUC resamples with explicit counts; train-versus-test population stability index (PSI) for all 12 point-in-time features and the chosen model's score distribution. PSI handles reference constants as unscorable rather than silently reporting zero drift, and rejects NaNs/undersized windows. PSI is not concept drift, causal bias, fairness or evidence of observed real fraud. No alert or retraining is triggered automatically. Entity overlap and zero-new-user cold-start blind spots remain explicitly flagged; fitted validation ECE is optimistic due to in-sample calibration. The model selected before calibration is not changed based on test metrics.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — P2 offline calibration and shift monitor
chunks.text: Review .github/workflows/p2-calibration-drift.yml for actual CPU-only unit + report acceptance and uploaded data. The pre-existing production-ish ml/monitoring/drift_detection.py has a permissive optional-Evidently fallback; this new path is separate and enforced, not an unsupported claim that production drift is now monitored. Next production gates are independently licensed datasets, shadow monitoring thresholds, preapproved rollback mechanics, enterprise reviewer auth and cloud deployment approval. Never use a fraud score as proof of wrongdoing or an automated denial.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Point-in-time graph-context features
chunks.text: Scope: local/synthetic events accepted by the real Kafka → Avro → SQLite ledger → Neo4j path. This milestone produces feature snapshots, not a trained fraud score, an analyst judgment, or a production feature store.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Point-in-time graph-context features
chunks.heading: Why the source ledger, not the current Neo4j graph?
chunks.text:
A live graph reflects transactions received after a past decision. A historical query against that graph can accidentally disclose future edges. data-eng/consumers/point_in_time_features.py therefore reconstructs user/device/merchant relationship counts from the first accepted normalized source records. These edges match the graph's source identities; the feature calculator does not pretend it executes GDS or a live Neo4j query.
The accepted local ledger stores receipt order (SQLite rowid), UTC receipt time, immutable transaction identity, event timestamp and normalized entities.
For a target transaction t, a historical record h is eligible only if:
h.ledger_rowid < t.first_ledger_rowid h.received_at_utc <= t.first_received_at_utc t.event_time_ms - window_ms <= h.event_time_ms < t.event_time_ms
The first two clauses prevent knowledge-time leakage (a late arrival or backfill cannot change a decision already made). The last clause prevents event-time leakage (a future event ingested early, or a simultaneous event, cannot become history). Time windows have an inclusive lower bound and exclusive upper bound. Neither fraud labels nor subsequent human review decisions are used.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Point-in-time graph-context features
chunks.heading: Feature contract: pit-v1
chunks.text:
- User transaction count in the previous 24 hours. - Same-currency user transaction count, amount sum and amount mean over 24h (no FX mixing, no made-up exchange rates). - Merchant transaction count over 24h. - Device transaction count, unique linked users and other linked users over 7 days. - Merchant distinct users over 7 days. - User→merchant transactions and user distinct devices over 30 days.
Zero-history results are explicit zero-valued features, not missing values filled by future knowledge.
The immutable table transaction_feature_snapshots contains a (transaction_id, feature_version) primary key, source payload SHA-256, event/receipt cutoffs, a canonical feature JSON and SHA-256, and computation time. It is written after graph projection and before Kafka offset acknowledgment. Restart/replay returns the first persisted snapshot; it does not silently recompute it after a late backfill. Failed snapshot materialization retains the Kafka offset for retry.

python -m pip install -r requirements-ci.txt pytest tests/unit/test_point_in_time_features.py tests/unit/test_graph_builder_delivery.py -v
Full Docker-backed source → features test:
python -m pip install -r requirements-ci.txt -r requirements-ingestion-ci.txt docker compose -f docker-compose.ingestion.yml up -d --wait GRAPHGUARD_INGESTION_INTEGRATION=1 pytest \ tests/integration/test_avro_registry.py -v docker compose -f docker-compose.ingestion.yml down --remove-orphans
One added Avro test ingests a historical transaction, an event whose event-time is in the future, and a target transaction; it checks the persisted target features. It then publishes an older-event-time transaction after the target decision and confirms that the snapshot hash stays unchanged. Existing real Kafka/Schema Registry/Neo4j integration tests also continue to run in CI.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Point-in-time graph-context features
chunks.heading: Limitations and following work
chunks.text: - This implementation scans synthetic records in a local SQLite DB. It is deliberately not a scalable distributed batch/stream feature platform, not Feast online materialization and not a performance claim. - First-seen knowledge comes from this one ledger. Reconstructing historical production knowledge requires authoritative ingestion logs, versioned entity resolution, a governed online/offline feature store and consistent retention policies. - Retrospective offline training on late-arriving data needs an explicit correction policy; it must not be confused with what the system knew at original decision time. Existing snapshots remain immutable. - The ledger contains synthetic IDs. No actual customer, IP or payment-card details should be inserted into this unauthenticated local fixture DB. - Currency comparison uses the same three-letter code only; exchange conversions, chargebacks, feature freshness SLAs and missing-data signals are not yet modeled. - Race/failure testing under concurrent multi-process consumers, Kafka rebalances, DB compaction and legacy migrations remains necessary. - Features are not used by a verified trained scoring model yet.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — Evidence-led portfolio copy (draft, not yet published)
chunks.heading: LinkedIn Featured description
chunks.text: GraphGuard is my applied ML and graph-data engineering portfolio project. I wanted to show how a suspicious transaction should become a reviewable investigation, rather than automatically being called fraud. The local test path ingests real Avro records through Kafka and Schema Registry, projects connections into Neo4j, and computes immutable graph features using only information known when a transaction arrived. I compared logistic regression and XGBoost on a deterministic synthetic chronological holdout, then built hash-verified scoring, native TreeSHAP explanations and signed analyst/admin case actions with a traceable local audit trail. A connected Next.js case desk exposes the model evidence and human review history without fake fallback scores. The results are synthetic research evidence, not real banking accuracy or a production deployment.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — Evidence-led portfolio copy (draft, not yet published)
chunks.heading: Case study (engineering narrative)
chunks.text:
Problem. A model can rank a transaction as unusual while hiding the data lineage, time leakage and review steps behind that score. I designed GraphGuard around an investigator's question: what was known, which relationships contributed to the model output, and who reviewed it?
Approach. The reproducible synthetic source uses a registered Avro transaction event, Kafka and Schema Registry, a durable first-observed SQLite ledger, and Neo4j user, device and merchant relationships. Point-in-time feature snapshots exclude information received after the scored event. Models are trained on chronological splits with an explicit feature allowlist and SHA-256 provenance; a model/feature mismatch fails closed.
Evaluation. I compared a standardized logistic regression baseline with XGBoost on simulated labels, recording PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, precision@K, calibration diagnostics and realized false-positive rates. XGBoost achieved a synthetic held-out PR-AUC of 0.7650, but its 9.375% held-out FPR exceeded the validation-selected 5% budget. That limitation matters more than presenting a flattering single score.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — Evidence-led portfolio copy (draft, not yet published)
chunks.heading: Case study (engineering narrative)
chunks.text:
Evaluation. I compared a standardized logistic regression baseline with XGBoost on simulated labels, recording PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, precision@K, calibration diagnostics and realized false-positive rates. XGBoost achieved a synthetic held-out PR-AUC of 0.7650, but its 9.375% held-out FPR exceeded the validation-selected 5% budget. That limitation matters more than presenting a flattering single score.
Investigation. Native TreeSHAP contributions reconstruct the actual model output in log odds. A signed local reviewer opens and escalates cases, while an admin can close them. Each review event is linked to immutable model/source/feature hashes and a local keyed audit chain. The Next.js case desk retrieves actual signed API data and makes clear what is synthetic.
Trade-offs. The quick-start seeds SQLite directly for accessibility; a separate Docker-backed integration test verifies Kafka through signed review. SQLite, demo tokens, an uncalibrated synthetic model and an unpublished cloud architecture are deliberately not described as production banking infrastructure.

chunks.title: GraphGuard — Evidence-led portfolio copy (draft, not yet published)
chunks.heading: A grounded technical interview story
chunks.text:
Question: What did you do to prevent fraud-label and future-event leakage? Answer: I constrained model input to an explicit point-in-time feature contract, recorded first-known transaction payloads in an immutable ledger, and snapshotted graph context using both event-time and observation-time cutoffs. Tests insert late-arriving events and replay Kafka to verify old snapshots do not change. Labels exist in the synthetic training dataset, not ledger or source features. I compare chronological splits and disclose repeated entities across train/test as an unresolved cold-start limitation.
Question: How do you know the explanation is real? Answer: I call native XGBoost TreeSHAP on the same hash-pinned model and exact 12 input columns that produced the saved score. I test that baseline plus contributions reconstructs the raw model margin and final score. The signed case anchors the explanation's SHA-256. Model attribution does not establish causality or a person's wrongdoing.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1/P2 — Reproducible baseline experiment (synthetic only)
chunks.heading: Purpose and provenance
chunks.text: The experiment in ml/training/pit_baselines.py trains both logistic regression and XGBoost using the real pit-v1 historical feature store. It uses in-repo deterministic synthetic-only data (seed 42; generator synthetic-ml-v1), with no downloaded third-party dataset, real fraud labels, provider API, paid AWS service or MLflow server. Synthetic labels are simulated scenarios, NOT confirmed wrongdoing. No external dataset licence is claimed; the repository's overall source licence requires a separate review.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1/P2 — Reproducible baseline experiment (synthetic only)
chunks.heading: Leakage and split controls
chunks.text: 1. Each synthetic event is written via TransactionLedger.record and snapshotted immediately by PointInTimeFeatureStore.snapshot_for. The generator's synthetic label stays outside the source ledger. 2. An explicit allowlist contains 11 pit-v1 historical features plus current amount (known at decision time). Input version: pit-v1+current-amount-v1. No IDs, future outcomes, targets, source rowids or human-review labels enter the model. 3. Train/validation/test = strict chronological 65/15/20. Duplicate IDs, tied boundary timestamps or single-class splits fail closed. Entities may reappear across periods, which models the same customer returning in a stream; IDs are excluded from features. Audit records entity overlaps. This is not an entity-disjoint cold-start test. 4. Logistic standardization and class balancing are trained on train only; XGBoost weighting uses train-only prevalence. No SMOTE or global normalization. Both models have fixed disclosed hyperparameters. 5. Winner = maximum validation average precision (PR-AUC). Decision threshold is selected using validation negatives to respect an FPR budget of 5%. Never select on the test set.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1/P2 — Reproducible baseline experiment (synthetic only)
chunks.heading: Inspectable measurements
chunks.text:
Each validation and test result includes average precision/PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, Brier score, 10-bin expected calibration error, precision@25, recall at validation-selected FPR, realized FPR and class prevalence. These are diagnostics, not claims of calibrated, fair or generalizable real-world fraud decisions. No model metrics are predeclared: use the precise CI-run artefact and log, not numbers in a proposal.
The generated manifest reports generator/version, dataset SHA-256, model JSON hashes, seed, feature columns, installed Python/numpy/sklearn/XGBoost versions, chronological split dates, entity overlap counts and scores.

Local generated files in .local/ml-baselines are ignored by Git: - synthetic_records.jsonl: inspectable synthetic dataset, with synthetic labels ONLY for offline evaluation; - logistic_baseline.json: safe JSON scaler coefficients and input order (not executable pickle); - xgboost_baseline.json: native XGBoost artifact, reloaded in a smoke test; - manifest.json: hashes and measured validation/test metrics.
CI's Synthetic point-in-time ML baselines job runs the tests and experiment and uploads the synthetic-only artifacts for 14 days. Those artifacts are not deployed.

Its leakage risk must be handled separately. The existing rigorous XGBoost and GAT implementations are NOT validated by this PR. Existing ml/serving/api.py uses a different feature namespace and may return fallbacks; do not silently deploy a model trained on pit-v1 into that API. Heuristic explanations are not SHAP.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Model-derived SHAP explanations, synthetic-only
chunks.text: Status: local research attribution for the exact hash-pinned model and immutable pit-v1 synthetic transaction snapshot. Not evidence of actual fraud, a causal explanation, a production scoring API, a calibrated risk estimate or an authenticated human decision.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Model-derived SHAP explanations, synthetic-only
chunks.heading: What is actually computed?
chunks.text: 1. Use the VerifiedSyntheticScorer introduced in PR #7. It must receive an independently trusted SHA-256 of the model manifest. The scorer verifies model bytes, feature order, source payload hash, point-in-time feature-snapshot hash, event and first-knowledge cutoffs, synthetic-only scope and GBP-only input. 2. Re-read the exact source and snapshot, recheck their hashes against the verified score and reconstruct the same ordered 12 input columns (pit-v1 historical graph features plus accepted current amount). No user ID, outcome, fraud label, IP or card fragment enters the explanation model. 3. XGBoost: call its real native Booster.predict(DMatrix, pred_contribs=True, approx_contribs=False) TreeSHAP algorithm. This is exact native tree-path-dependent TreeSHAP for the trained model; no randomly generated importance, heuristic thresholds, sampled fake SHAP, or fitted external explainer. Its reported baseline is the trained booster path-dependent log-odds baseline, not a causal or population reference. 4. Logistic regression: use the exact additive Shapley decomposition for the standardized linear logit model relative to the saved training feature means: (value - training_mean) / training_scale × coefficient.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Model-derived SHAP explanations, synthetic-only
chunks.heading: What is actually computed?
chunks.text: The frozen intercept is the baseline log-odds. This is a training-mean additive reference; correlated-feature/conditional attribution is not inferred. 5. Both paths operate on log odds, not percentage-point probability changes. baseline_log_odds + sum(feature_SHAP_log_odds) reconstructs the raw prediction; stable sigmoid reconstruction must match the independently verified model probability to within 2e-5. An incorrect shape, nonfinite value or inconsistent reconstruction fails closed. 6. Return ranked top-K signed numeric attributions (absolute-value descending, stable feature-name tie-break), all feature contributions, model/manifest/source/feature SHA-256 references, feature-input/explainer version, reconstruction error and a conspicuous non-causality warning. 7. Optional local SQLite research persistence requires a matching already verified saved score. The writer recomputes the entire explanation with the pinned scorer before the first INSERT. Exact Kafka replay is idempotent and cannot overwrite a previously different explanation for the same (transaction_id, manifest, explainer_version).

The --persist-research-artifacts flag is optional and writes a locally revalidated research score + explanation, not an operational case, accusation or reviewer decision.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Model-derived SHAP explanations, synthetic-only
chunks.heading: Hard limitations
chunks.text: - Shapley contributions are model attributions, not causal evidence or real-fraud proof. A large positive log-odds contribution is not a human judgment or policy threshold. - The previous synthetic XGBoost validation FPR target of 5% produced 9.375% test FPR. The model is not safe for automated declines, and these explanations do not change that. - TreeSHAP uses the booster tree-path-dependent background, not an external independent baseline; correlated features may redistribute credit. Logistic values use a training-mean baseline without dependency modeling. - This is a local deterministic synthetic proof: no production data, third-party dataset validation, SHAP fairness guarantee, runtime performance SLA, full dependency lockfile, live API integration, or secured model registry. - A hash is integrity evidence only. A separately supplied pin is the trust boundary; an attacker with unrestricted local filesystem or SQLite write privileges can rewrite the research data.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Model-derived SHAP explanations, synthetic-only

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Trust-pinned synthetic feature → model inference
chunks.heading: Inference boundary
chunks.text: 1. A transaction must first be accepted by the real Kafka Avro consumer and materialized in the SQLite first-seen source ledger. GraphBuilder writes its pit-v1 feature snapshot before committing the Kafka source offset. 2. A separately trained synthetic Logistic Regression/XGBoost artifact and manifest.json are produced by the PR #6 baseline experiment. The caller must pass the trusted 64-character SHA-256 of the manifest obtained through an approved build/CI channel. Calculating the pin from an untrusted manifest at score time is not a trust boundary. 3. VerifiedSyntheticScorer verifies manifest SHA-256, exact synthetic scope, selected model artifact SHA-256, feature column ordering and input version pit-v1+current-amount-v1, then loads the native XGBoost or safe JSON logistic model. No pickle or arbitrary code loader is used. 4. Each inference verifies accepted source payload hash, schema version, GBP-only synthetic scope, immutable feature-snapshot hash, original receipt/event-time cutoffs, feature version and the exact 11 historical numeric features. Current amount comes only from the accepted source payload. Any mismatch fails closed. 5.

chunks.title: GraphGuard P1 — Trust-pinned synthetic feature → model inference
chunks.heading: Inference boundary
chunks.text: A numeric model score is returned with model name, artifact/manifest/source/feature hashes, feature version and RESEARCH_SCORE_ONLY_NO_AUTOMATED_DECISION. The score is an uncalibrated synthetic model output, never proof of wrongdoing. Optional save_research_score first recalculates the proposed score with a verified pinned scorer, then appends one local research record per transaction+manifest. Unverified first writes and attempts to overwrite a previous score are rejected; replay is idempotent.

chunks.text:
Before an authorised real plan/apply: obtain explicit approval for account, regional provider pricing (default eu-west-2), unique bucket, existing reviewed OIDC-provider ARN, protected GitHub environment, remote state backend and retention/privacy policy. Use AWS Pricing Calculator. Athena is charged per data scanned; 1 GiB cutoff is per query, not a monthly budget. At an illustrative $5/TB, 100 maximum-size queries correspond to roughly 0.1 TB / $0.50 of scan volume alone; this is not a quoted actual bill. Set AWS Budgets alerts (not hard caps) and avoid uploading data before approval. force_destroy = false prevents accidental nonempty bucket deletion; any teardown must be explicitly approved, preserving evidence, IAM roles and remote state.
Full operational production scope requires independently authorised OIDC, real role testing, secret management, provider endpoints, incident monitoring, encrypted audit retention and identity management. Human-review fraud scores remain synthetic and are never an automated final judgement.

chunks.title: GraphGuard README
chunks.heading: Case opening / One event is not the whole story
chunks.text:
Consider a fictional example: a purchase looks routine on its own, but the device appears on several accounts, which in turn connect to related merchants. Those relationships deserve inspection—not an automatic verdict.
Can we reveal the context behind a suspicious transaction, explain the model's reasoning and help an analyst decide what to examine next?
GraphGuard's codebase explores that question. It separates evidence, model output, explanation and reviewer action. Some of the implementation is modular or local-first; not every service in the architectural vision is active in the hosted demo.

chunks.title: ADR 001: Use TimescaleDB for Price History Storage
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
Sentinance needs to store time-series price data for: - 8 assets (4 crypto + 4 market indices) - Multiple time granularities (tick, 1m, 1h, 1d) - 5+ years of historical data for ML training - Real-time ingestion with sub-second latency
This results in approximately: - 21M+ rows per year (8 assets × 365 days × 1440 minutes) - 100M+ rows for 5-year training data

chunks.title: ADR 001: Use TimescaleDB for Price History Storage
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Use TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension) instead of: - Regular PostgreSQL - InfluxDB - MongoDB

chunks.title: ADR 001: Use TimescaleDB for Price History Storage
chunks.heading: Rationale
chunks.text:
Why TimescaleDB?: 1. Automatic Partitioning: Hypertables automatically partition by time 2. SQL Compatibility: Full PostgreSQL SQL support (joins, CTEs, window functions) 3. Compression: 10-20x compression ratio for time-series data 4. Continuous Aggregates: Pre-computed OHLCV rollups (hourly, daily) 5. Mature Ecosystem: Production-ready, extensive documentation
Alternatives Considered: Database · Pros · Cons · DecisionInfluxDB · Purpose-built for time-series · InfluxQL learning curve, no joins · Rejected PostgreSQL · Familiar, reliable · Manual partitioning, no time-series optimizations · Rejected MongoDB · Flexible schema · Not optimized for time-series, aggregations slower · Rejected QuestDB · Very fast ingestion · Less mature, smaller community · Rejected

chunks.title: ADR 001: Use TimescaleDB for Price History Storage
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Fast time-range queries (automatic index on time) - Pre-computed aggregates reduce query load - Can use existing SQLAlchemy ORM with minor changes - Built-in retention policies for data lifecycle
Negative: - Requires TimescaleDB-specific knowledge - Slightly more complex than vanilla PostgreSQL - Additional Docker image size (~200MB)

chunks.title: ADR 001: Use TimescaleDB for Price History Storage
chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.text: Implementation: -- Create hypertable SELECT create_hypertable('price_history', 'time', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 day'); -- Continuous aggregate for hourly OHLCV CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW price_hourly WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS bucket, symbol, first(price, time) as open, max(price) as high, min(price) as low, last(price, time) as close, sum(volume) as volume FROM price_history GROUP BY bucket, symbol;

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance needs to calculate technical indicators for 8 assets: - RSI (Relative Strength Index) - MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) - Bollinger Bands - Moving Averages (SMA, EMA) - ATR (Average True Range) These calculations must be: - Accurate (match industry-standard formulas) - Fast (<50ms per calculation) - Maintainable (clear, testable code)

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Implement indicators in-house using NumPy instead of: - TA-Lib (C library with Python bindings) - pandas-ta - tulipy

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Rationale
chunks.text: Why In-House?: 1. Full Control: Understand every line of the algorithm 2. No Dependencies: Avoid C library compilation issues 3. Educational Value: Portfolio project demonstrates understanding 4. Customization: Easy to modify for specific use cases

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Rationale > Key Implementation Details > MACD Signal Line (Critical Fix)
chunks.text:
The signal line MUST be the 9-period EMA of MACD history, NOT a simplified approximation.
Wrong (Bug Fixed):
signal_line = macd_line * 0.9 # ❌ WRONG
Correct:
# Calculate MACD history macd_history = [] for i in range(slow, len(prices) + 1): ema_fast = calculate_ema(prices[:i], fast) ema_slow = calculate_ema(prices[:i], slow) macd_history.append(ema_fast - ema_slow)
# Signal line is EMA of MACD history signal_line = calculate_ema(macd_history, signal) # ✅ CORRECT

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Rationale > Key Implementation Details
chunks.text: RSI Calculation: RSI = 100 - (100 / (1 + RS)) RS = Average Gain / Average Loss over N periods The implementation uses a 14-period lookback by default.

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Zero external dependencies for calculations - 100% test coverage achievable - Clear documentation of each formula - Easy to add new indicators
Negative: - More code to maintain than using a library - Potential for bugs (mitigated by comprehensive tests) - Less optimized than C-based TA-Lib

chunks.title: ADR 003: Technical Indicator Calculation Strategy
chunks.heading: Test Coverage
chunks.text: Test Coverage: class TestMACD: def test_macd_signal_is_not_simplified(self, prices): """Signal line should NOT be MACD * 0.9""" macd, signal, histogram = calculate_macd(prices) assert abs(signal - macd * 0.9) > 0.001 # ✅

chunks.title: ADR 004: Kafka for Event Streaming
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance needs to handle: - Real-time price updates from multiple exchanges - Event-driven architecture for alerts and notifications - Decoupled services for horizontal scaling - Message persistence for replay capability Current implementation uses Redis Pub/Sub, which works but has limitations.

chunks.title: ADR 004: Kafka for Event Streaming
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Add Apache Kafka for event streaming alongside Redis Pub/Sub. Architecture: Exchange APIs → Kafka → Consumers (API, Alerts, Analytics) ↓ Redis (cache, fast pub/sub for WebSocket)

chunks.title: ADR 004: Kafka for Event Streaming
chunks.heading: Rationale
chunks.text:
Why Kafka?: Feature · Redis Pub/Sub · KafkaMessage persistence · ❌ No · ✅ Configurable retention Replay capability · ❌ No · ✅ Consumer can seek Horizontal scaling · ⚠️ Limited · ✅ Partitions Message ordering · ✅ Yes · ✅ Per partition Throughput · 100K msg/s · 1M+ msg/s
When to Use Each: Use Case · Technology · ReasonWebSocket to clients · Redis Pub/Sub · Low latency, ephemeral Price ingestion · Kafka · Persistence, replay Alert triggers · Kafka · Reliable delivery Analytics events · Kafka · Batch processing

chunks.title: ADR 004: Kafka for Event Streaming
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Message durability (no data loss on service restart) - Horizontal scaling with consumer groups - Event replay for debugging and analytics - Decoupled architecture
Negative: - Additional infrastructure complexity - JVM-based (higher memory footprint) - Learning curve for operations

chunks.title: ADR 005: Graceful Degradation for Demo Mode
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance has two deployment modes: 1. Local/Production: Full stack with all services 2. Demo/Free-tier: Simplified deployment on Vercel/Railway The demo mode should work with limited infrastructure while clearly indicating what features are unavailable.

chunks.title: ADR 005: Graceful Degradation for Demo Mode
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Implement graceful degradation patterns throughout the codebase so one codebase works in both modes.

chunks.title: ADR 005: Graceful Degradation for Demo Mode
chunks.heading: Implementation Patterns
chunks.text:
Pattern 1: Try/Except Imports: try: from kafka import KafkaProducer KAFKA_AVAILABLE = True except ImportError: KAFKA_AVAILABLE = False # Usage if KAFKA_AVAILABLE: producer.send('topics', message) else: await redis.publish('channel', message)
Pattern 2: Environment Detection: def is_production() -> bool: return os.getenv("ENVIRONMENT") == "production" def get_database_url() -> str: if is_production(): return os.getenv("TIMESCALEDB_URL") # Full TimescaleDB return os.getenv("DATABASE_URL") # Regular PostgreSQL/Supabase
Pattern 3: Feature Flags: FEATURES = { "kafka": os.getenv("KAFKA_ENABLED", "false").lower() == "true", "mlflow": os.getenv("MLFLOW_ENABLED", "false").lower() == "true", "tracing": os.getenv("JAEGER_ENABLED", "false").lower() == "true", }
Pattern 4: Fallback Responses: async def get_prediction(symbol: str) -> dict: try: # Try ML model return await ml_model.predict(symbol) except ModelNotAvailable: # Fallback to rule-based return await rule_based_prediction(symbol)

chunks.title: ADR 005: Graceful Degradation for Demo Mode

chunks.title: ADR 006: WebSocket Architecture with Redis Pub/Sub
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance requires real-time price streaming to connected clients with: - Sub-100ms latency - Support for 1000+ concurrent connections - Horizontal scaling across multiple API instances

chunks.title: ADR 006: WebSocket Architecture with Redis Pub/Sub
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Use Redis Pub/Sub as the message broker for WebSocket distribution.

chunks.title: ADR 006: WebSocket Architecture with Redis Pub/Sub
chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.text: Architecture: Exchange APIs ↓ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Price Stream │ (Background Task) │ Service │ └──────────────────┘ ↓ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Redis Pub/Sub │ (Channel: prices) └──────────────────┘ ↓ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │ API Instance 1 │ API Instance 2 │ │ (WebSocket) │ (WebSocket) │ └──────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ Clients

chunks.title: ADR 006: WebSocket Architecture with Redis Pub/Sub
chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.text: Implementation: class ConnectionManager: def init(self): self.active_connections: List[WebSocket] = [] self.redis = redis.Redis() async def broadcast_from_redis(self): pubsub = self.redis.pubsub() await pubsub.subscribe("prices") async for message in pubsub.listen(): if message["type"] == "message": await self.broadcast(message["data"])

chunks.title: ADR 006: WebSocket Architecture with Redis Pub/Sub
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Horizontal scaling (any instance can serve any client) - Low latency (<50ms) - Simple implementation - Built-in with existing Redis
Negative: - No message persistence (acceptable for price streaming) - At-most-once delivery

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance needs authentication for: - Protected API endpoints (alerts, user preferences) - Rate limiting by user tier - Audit logging

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Use JWT (JSON Web Tokens) with: - Short-lived access tokens (30 minutes) - Refresh token rotation - bcrypt password hashing

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Token Structure
chunks.text: Token Structure: { "sub": "user-uuid", "email": "user@example.com", "is_premium": false, "exp": 1706000000, "iat": 1706000000 }

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.text: Implementation: from jose import jwt from passlib.context import CryptContext pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto") def create_access_token(data: dict, expires_delta: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=30)): to_encode = data.copy() expire = datetime.utcnow() + expires_delta to_encode.update({"exp": expire}) return jwt.encode(to_encode, SECRET_KEY, algorithm="HS256") def verify_token(token: str) -> dict: return jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=["HS256"])

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Stateless (no session storage needed) - Works with load balancing - Self-contained user info
Negative: - Token revocation requires blocklist - Larger than session cookies

chunks.title: ADR 007: JWT Authentication Strategy
chunks.heading: Security Considerations
chunks.text: Security Considerations: - JWT_SECRET must be 256+ bits - Never store in localStorage (use httpOnly cookies) - Validate exp claim on every request

chunks.title: ADR 008: Prometheus Metrics Strategy
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Need observability for: - API performance (latency, throughput) - Business metrics (predictions served, chat sessions) - Infrastructure health (Redis, DB connections)

chunks.title: ADR 008: Prometheus Metrics Strategy
chunks.heading: Metrics Defined
chunks.text: Metric · Type · Labels · Descriptionsentinance_requests_total · Counter · method, endpoint, status · Total requests sentinance_request_latency_seconds · Histogram · method, endpoint · Request duration sentinance_websocket_connections · Gauge · - · Active WS connections sentinance_prediction_latency_seconds · Histogram · model, horizon · ML prediction time sentinance_chat_latency_seconds · Histogram · model · AI chat response time sentinance_errors_total · Counter · type, endpoint · Error count

chunks.title: ADR 008: Prometheus Metrics Strategy
chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.text: Implementation: from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, Gauge REQUEST_COUNT = Counter('sentinance_requests_total', 'Total requests', ['method', 'endpoint', 'status']) REQUEST_LATENCY = Histogram('sentinance_request_latency_seconds', 'Request latency', ['method', 'endpoint'], buckets=[0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0])

chunks.title: ADR 008: Prometheus Metrics Strategy
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Industry standard (Grafana integration) - Low overhead - Pull-based (no push infrastructure needed)
Negative: - Cardinality explosion risk with high-cardinality labels - Requires Prometheus server running

chunks.title: ADR 008: Prometheus Metrics Strategy
chunks.heading: Grafana Queries
chunks.text: Grafana Queries: # Request rate by endpoint sum(rate(sentinance_requests_total[5m])) by (endpoint) # P99 latency histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(sentinance_request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]))

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance needs price prediction for: - 1-hour, 24-hour, 7-day horizons - Multiple assets (crypto + indices) - Confidence scores for user guidance

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Use LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) neural networks trained on historical price data.

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Model Architecture
chunks.text: Model Architecture: Input (60 timesteps, 1 feature) ↓ LSTM (128 units, return_sequences=True) ↓ Dropout (0.2) ↓ LSTM (64 units) ↓ Dropout (0.2) ↓ Dense (64, ReLU) ↓ Dense (1, Linear) ↓ Output (predicted price)

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Training Pipeline
chunks.text: Training Pipeline: # 1. Download 5 years of hourly data df = yf.Ticker("BTC-USD").history(period="5y", interval="1h") # 2. Normalize with Min-Max scaling prices_normalized = (prices - min) / (max - min) # 3. Create sequences (60 timesteps lookback) X, y = create_sequences(prices_normalized, lookback=60) # 4. Train with 70/15/15 split model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=50, validation_data=(X_val, y_val)) # 5. Log to MLflow mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, "model")

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Captures temporal patterns - Proven for time-series - PyTorch integration with MLflow
Negative: - Training time (30-60 min per model) - Requires retraining for market regime changes - GPU beneficial but not required

chunks.title: ADR 009: LSTM for Price Prediction
chunks.heading: Fallback
chunks.text: Fallback: When trained model unavailable, use ensemble of: - Momentum prediction - Mean reversion if not model_available: return ensemble_prediction(momentum, mean_reversion)

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text: Context: Sentinance backend needs: - High-performance REST API - WebSocket support for real-time streaming - Async I/O for concurrent exchange API calls - Automatic OpenAPI documentation

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Decision
chunks.text: Decision: Use FastAPI as the primary backend framework.

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Rationale
chunks.text: Feature · FastAPI · Flask · DjangoAsync native · ✅ · ⚠️ (with extensions) · ⚠️ (with ASGI) WebSocket · ✅ Built-in · ❌ Needs extension · ⚠️ Channels OpenAPI docs · ✅ Auto-generated · ❌ Manual · ⚠️ With DRF Performance · ~10K req/s · ~2K req/s · ~1K req/s Type hints · ✅ Required · ⚠️ Optional · ⚠️ Optional

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Key Features Used
chunks.text: Key Features Used: 1. Async Endpoints: For non-blocking exchange API calls 2. Dependency Injection: For auth, database sessions 3. Pydantic Models: For request/response validation 4. Background Tasks: For price streaming 5. WebSocket: For real-time client updates

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Implementation Pattern
chunks.text: Implementation Pattern: from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, WebSocket, BackgroundTasks app = FastAPI(title="Sentinance API") @app.get("/api/prices/{symbol}") async def get_price(symbol: str, user: User = Depends(get_current_user)): return await exchange.get_price(symbol) @app.websocket("/ws/prices") async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket): await manager.connect(websocket)

chunks.title: ADR 010: FastAPI as Backend Framework
chunks.heading: Consequences
chunks.text:
Positive: - Excellent developer experience - Auto-generated docs at /docs - Native async for high concurrency - Type safety with Pydantic
Negative: - Smaller ecosystem than Django - Less batteries-included

chunks.title: Data Lineage Documentation
chunks.text: Evidence boundary (P1 draft, 16 November 2026): The diagram below describes an intended architecture, not a verified production market-source → Kafka → Parquet/dbt → ML → browser path. Existing price_stream_task() fetches into in-memory caches and publishes via Redis; it does not automatically produce Kafka records. Draft PR #31 introduces a separately activated, versioned sentinance.prices.v1 producer and Kafka → PostgreSQL raw-event sink with replay-safe keys, backed by a real broker/database CI test. Parquet, dbt, Spark, Feast, MLflow, provider licensing, model evaluation and the complete browser journey remain unverified until independently tested. Latency SLAs below are targets, not measured guarantees. For the actual v1 event contract, migration and recovery semantics, see P1 durable price ledger.

chunks.heading: Transformation Pipeline
chunks.text:
Stage 1: Raw Ingestion: - Location: apps/api/multi_exchange.py - Output: Raw price ticks with timestamps - Schema: symbol: string (PK) price: float volume: float change_24h: float timestamp: datetime exchange: string
Stage 2: Kafka Events: - Location: apps/api/kafka_producer.py - Topic: sentinance.prices - Format: JSON - Partitioning: By symbol
Stage 3: dbt Staging: - Location: apps/dbt/models/staging/stg_prices.sql - Materialization: Incremental - Transformations: - Type casting - Deduplication - Null handling
Stage 4: dbt Marts: - Location: apps/dbt/models/marts/ - Tables: - mart_daily_metrics - OHLCV aggregations - mart_technical_indicators - RSI, MACD, Bollinger
Stage 5: Feature Engineering: - Location: apps/spark/spark_features.py - Features: - Moving averages (SMA, EMA) - RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands - Time-based features (hour, day_of_week) - Volume features (ratio, change)
Stage 6: Feature Store: - Location: apps/feature_store/feature_store.py - Backend: Feast (local SQLite) - Feature Views: - price_features - Real-time prices - technical_indicators - TA indicators - market_features - Market aggregates

chunks.text: The pre-existing ticker/price-stream code takes local fetch timestamps and does not carry a stable upstream event identity. chunks.title: P1 — Source-identifiable aggregate trades (fixture and opt-in provider)
chunks.heading: Why the original 24-hour ticker is not sufficient
chunks.text: - Topic: sentinance.prices.v1 (same opt-in durable topic as PR #31) - Sources: binance_aggtrade for opt-in real provider requests and binance_aggtrade_fixture for synthetic HTTP fixtures; these identities intentionally cannot collide in the durable ledger - Identity: (source, symbol, aggregate trade ID) in PostgreSQL - Timestamp: T from provider, normalized to UTC - Provenance: explicit mode=fixture in offline CI and seeded demos, mode=provider only in the opt-in live CLI. All new fixture records use a different source namespace from real provider records - Fetch: one bounded REST page using a known fromId, up to 1000 records; validates every record and strict aggregate-trade ID continuity before sending any Kafka records - Failure: missing/duplicated/out-of-order IDs fail closed; transport and HTTP 5xx errors use at most three bounded jittered attempts. HTTP 418/429 and other 4xx fail immediately. An interrupted Kafka publish can leave an acknowledged prefix: rerun using the same upstream IDs and rely on the transactional source/symbol/event ID key rather than a made-up exactly-once claim.

chunks.title: P1: durable Kafka → PostgreSQL price-event ledger
chunks.heading: Implemented path
chunks.text:
Explicit fixture/source event (stable source event_id, observed time) -> PriceProducer.send_price_v1() [broker ack, acks=all] -> Kafka topic sentinance.prices.v1 [JSON schema_version=1] -> PriceConsumer [manual Kafka commits; dedicated group] -> DurablePriceSink [PostgreSQL transaction; unique source ID and Kafka offset] -> Kafka offset commit ONLY after PostgreSQL commit
Example synthetic event, not an observed exchange quote:
{ "type": "price_update", "schema_version": 1, "source": "fixture_exchange", "event_id": "synthetic-stable-tick-001", "symbol": "BTCUSDT", "timestamp": "2026-11-16T10:00:00+00:00", "data": { "price": "101.25", "volume": "2" } }
The timestamp is supplied by the event source, not fabricated at ingestion; naive times, invalid schema versions, nonfinite/nonpositive prices, negative volumes and values outside PostgreSQL NUMERIC(30,12) are rejected. The insertion timestamp is recorded separately as received_at.
The Postgres table raw_kafka_price_events is append-only for accepted events, with primary key (topic, partition, offset) and a unique (source, symbol, source_event_id) constraint. Replayed records and republished events with the same source/symbol event ID and identical payload do not create duplicates. If either idempotency key is reused with different content, the consumer fails, leaving the Kafka record unacknowledged for operator investigation.

chunks.title: P1: durable Kafka → PostgreSQL price-event ledger
chunks.heading: Local or isolated execution (manual opt-in only)
chunks.text:
1. Supply a real isolated DATABASE_URL using the asyncpg dialect (postgresql+asyncpg://...) and a locally accessible Kafka broker via KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS. 2. Inside apps/api, apply alembic upgrade head to that isolated PostgreSQL database. Do not run this against production without a reviewed migration plan. 3. Start the standalone worker with P1_DURABLE_PRICE_SINK_ENABLED=1 python durable_price_worker.py. It does not start unless explicitly enabled. 4. To create synthetic smoke events use PriceProducer.send_price_v1(source=..., event_id=..., symbol=..., observed_at=..., price=..., volume=...). Reuse the same source ID when retrying the same source event. 5. Query raw_kafka_price_events; inspect actual Kafka group offsets and logs before considering a replay test successful.
This worker is deliberately not enabled in main.py or Kubernetes manifests. Deploying it requires separate consumer lifecycle, secret handling, database migration, broker quotas and resource review. Neither duplicate rejection nor replay can reconstruct provider observations that never reached Kafka.

chunks.title: P1: durable Kafka → PostgreSQL price-event ledger
chunks.heading: Verified vs open
chunks.text: The dedicated CI workflow .github/workflows/p1-durable-kafka-postgres.yml uses disposable Kafka and PostgreSQL, applies the real Alembic migration and injects a consumer crash after storing an event but before committing the Kafka offset. A restarted consumer must replay the uncommitted record; another broker publication with the same source event ID must leave exactly one database row. These checks prove a local at-least-once processing contract backed by a transactional idempotent sink, not a Kafka/PostgreSQL atomic transaction or exactly-once system-wide delivery.

chunks.title: P1: durable Kafka → PostgreSQL price-event ledger
chunks.heading: Source adapter milestone — stacked draft PR #34 (17 November 2026)
chunks.text:
apps/api/market_event_sources.py adds a bounded, read-only adapter to Binance Spot GET /api/v3/aggTrades. It preserves upstream aggregate trade ID (a), source execution timestamp (T in milliseconds), price (p) and aggregated base-quantity (q). These events are aggregate trades, not 24-hour ticker snapshots and not uninterrupted live market coverage. An explicit inclusive fromId is required; there is no inferred or fabricated source event ID. An observed gap, duplicate or reordered ID aborts publication for that page; HTTP 429/403/5xx and Kafka-delivery faults propagate to the operator.
A bounded source page can contain at most 1,000 rows, and a manually invoked batch allows up to 10 pages. Each event awaits a Kafka broker acknowledgment before the next record is sent. The returned next cursor is in-memory output only, not committed alongside Kafka or stored in a source-checkpoint table. On an interrupted batch, restart from a known earlier ID; database uniqueness makes repeat publications safe. This does not solve Kafka retention, late arrivals or historical gaps when upstream data is no longer accessible.

chunks.title: P1: durable Kafka → PostgreSQL price-event ledger
chunks.heading: Source adapter milestone — stacked draft PR #34 (17 November 2026)

A single bounded CLI command is: python market_source_worker.py --symbol BTCUSDT --from-id <trusted-ID> --page-size 100 --max-pages 1. The existing price_stream_task() is unchanged.
Reference: official Binance Spot aggregate trades documentation and Spot REST API base-URL guidance.

chunks.title: P1 — Reproduce source → Kafka → PostgreSQL → API → browser
chunks.heading: Proven and inspectable boundaries
chunks.text:
Synthetic aggregate-trade fixture (clearly mode=fixture) -> httpx.MockTransport (no provider network call) -> strict Binance aggregate-trade adapter (source ID and UTC time) -> Kafka sentinance.prices.v1 (broker acknowledged) -> durable PostgreSQL transaction (source+symbol+ID unique) -> FastAPI GET /api/v1/market-events -> Next.js /data/evidence (Zod parsed, never fakes a missing API)
The source field for fixture events is binance_aggtrade_fixture, while explicitly enabled real requests use binance_aggtrade. This prevents fixture IDs from colliding with real provider IDs in the same database. The provider timestamp is sourced from the trade response; only the database received_at clock is local.
The API returns only a bounded read-only slice (up to 50 events), including raw decimal strings, observed_at, received_at, source event identity, fixture/provider/unverified origin and recent/stale/future_timestamp freshness. It always returns live_feed_verified=false: a source field or recent timestamp does not confirm an actively connected exchange.

docker compose -f infra/docker-compose.yml up -d postgres redpanda
2. In apps/api create a Python 3.11 environment, install requirements, and configure only local connection strings:

chunks.title: P1 local Parquet evidence snapshots
chunks.text: Status: review-only PR #35. This is an offline, local data-lake slice, not an S3/AWS deployment or proof of exchange licensing. The user-facing site, model and agent are not connected.

chunks.title: P1 local Parquet evidence snapshots
chunks.heading: Reproducible path
chunks.text:
The focused integration workflow uses a synthetic aggregate-trade HTTP fixture, a real disposable Kafka broker, and real disposable PostgreSQL. It publishes source-owned versioned events, persists them with consumer-position/source-ID uniqueness, then exports the PostgreSQL raw-event ledger into three local Parquet files:
synthetic HTTP aggregate trade with stable upstream ID ↓ validate source fields (ID, price, quantity, observed UTC time) Kafka sentinance.prices.v1 → broker ack ↓ PostgreSQL raw_kafka_price_events → unique source/symbol/event ID ↓ local immutable snapshot directory (SHA-256 content address) ├── raw/raw.parquet Kafka position + upstream raw JSON ├── validated/validated.parquet typed source/time/price/quantity ├── curated/minute_bars.parquet UTC-minute OHLCV and trade-qty VWAP └── manifest.json row counts, time range, file checksums
A 1-minute bar groups aggregate trades by source, instrument and observed UTC minute. Price columns use PostgreSQL/Arrow-compatible decimal precision rather than early floating-point coercion. The base_volume is aggregate trade base quantity, not dollar volume. VWAP is weighted by this source quantity, not a future-looking forecast. Missing or zero volume gives null VWAP.

chunks.title: P1 local Parquet evidence snapshots
chunks.heading: Reproducible path
chunks.text:
A 1-minute bar groups aggregate trades by source, instrument and observed UTC minute. Price columns use PostgreSQL/Arrow-compatible decimal precision rather than early floating-point coercion. The base_volume is aggregate trade base quantity, not dollar volume. VWAP is weighted by this source quantity, not a future-looking forecast. Missing or zero volume gives null VWAP.
The exporter revalidates stored source JSON against the materialized PostgreSQL columns. A mismatched, nonfinite or malformed source record blocks export. Files are written to a staging directory then the completed snapshot directory is renamed into place. Data snapshots are content-addressed and immutable: a late event generates a different snapshot, retaining earlier versions for comparison. Each manifest includes SHA-256 file hashes, and verify_snapshot checks all three expected layers before accepting a snapshot.

chunks.title: P2 chronological ridge AR(1) evaluation
chunks.text:
The baseline evaluator and trainable ridge AR(1) use the same verified local curated Parquet snapshot and same held-out timestamps. A model observes the past log return and predicts the next log return. Hyperparameters are fixed candidates; select by validation MAE, ties prefer larger regularization. Refit once on all pre-test targets. Test uses rolling observed history, fixed coefficients; no test fitting or selection. Compare last-close, five-bar mean and ridge using MAE/RMSE/mean error. No resampling gaps, future target features, or implied trade profitability. JSON is deterministic within an identical runtime and exclusive output creation prevents accidental overwrite. The printed SHA-256 identifies the report. Model version, coefficients, split timestamps, source, snapshot ID, manifest hash and predictions are in the report.
Example from apps/api (operator supplies independent manifest hash and explicit boundaries): python forecast_model.py /path/to/snapshot --manifest-sha256 HASH --source fixture_exchange --symbol BTCUSDT --train-end 12 --validation-end 18 --output report.json

chunks.title: P2 chronological ridge AR(1) evaluation
chunks.text:
CI synthetic cases check known trends and constant prices, invalid splits, leakage by mutating test values, and pinned Parquet provenance. Not evidence of real-market predictive performance, live arrival-time availability, LSTM superiority, or fully secured ML registry. A historical market dataset with verified rights, arrival timestamps, out-of-sample comparison and deployment review remain necessary.
Prior P1 receipt and repair test 44726728919 passed 26 tests. Quality run reported two formatting differences, fixed in this batch. Exact head CI must report success before release.
The dedicated acceptance workflow uploads the synthetic pinned-Parquet forecast JSON and SHA-256 digest as synthetic-pinned-parquet-forecast-report (14-day retention). These contain fixture data only, not live market performance. The older Ruff 0.1.8 gate also found five E721 type-comparison violations despite modern lint passing; use explicit bool rejection with isinstance, preserving strict integer validation rather than suppressing the checks.

chunks.title: P2 — Forecast uncertainty and bounded synthetic benchmark
chunks.text: The historical ridge-log-return AR(1) test report is compared on the same held-out targets to last close and trailing mean; no test-period hyperparameter selection occurs. forecast_quality.py recomputes per-method MAE, RMSE, median/p95/max absolute error from the actual held-out predictions (it does not trust cached summary metrics). It reports a signed paired MAE delta (model minus last-close baseline) and an explicit underperformance flag. The fixed-seed 250-repetition moving-block bootstrap uses consecutive blocks of up to five held-out minutes; its percentiles are heuristics, particularly with small sample sizes and serial dependence. This is not calibrated model confidence, a formal performance guarantee or evidence of profitable trading.

chunks.title: P2 — Forecast uncertainty and bounded synthetic benchmark
chunks.text:
benchmark_forecast_quality.py builds 3000 deterministic UTC contiguous fixture minutes, with 1500 training observations, 500 validation observations and 1000 held-out test observations, and prints measured elapsed milliseconds and error summaries from the CI runner. The 15-second limit is a deliberately loose CI regression budget, not a production latency SLA. Runtime depends on the runner; inspect the JSON attached to the forecast-evaluation workflow. Use cd apps/api && python -m benchmark_forecast_quality to repeat offline.
For an independently pinned operator-approved report, run python forecast_quality.py /path/report.json --sha256 PINNED_REPORT_HASH --output unique-quality.json. Any failed hash, invalid/small report or invalid/NaN predictions fails closed. No real licensed dataset, trading strategy, transaction fees, distributed monitoring or automated drift retraining is asserted. We do not compute trading returns from a next-close regression, since a trading policy would require its own timing, spread/fee/slippage and market-impact assumptions.

chunks.text: One-line recruiter tagline: Built a traceable crypto-market investigation prototype using versioned Kafka events, a PostgreSQL ledger, immutable Parquet/dbt analytics, leakage-aware forecasting and a constrained LangGraph evidence trail — verified end-to-end with synthetic data in CI.

chunks.title: Sentinance — interview-ready claims (source-backed)
chunks.heading: LinkedIn Featured description (draft; publish only after final checks)
chunks.text: Sentinance is my AI-systems and time-series data engineering project. I wanted to explore a practical question: can a market-intelligence product show exactly where its facts come from? I built a synthetic-source replay through Kafka and PostgreSQL, exported checksum-verified Parquet snapshots, and ran dbt models with data-quality tests. A chronological forecasting benchmark compares a simple statistical model against last-price and moving-average baselines. A constrained LangGraph path reads a pinned evaluation report, recomputes metrics, and produces a traceable citation without inventing live prices. GitHub CI runs the full fixture journey in Chromium, including a deliberately corrupted report that the UI rejects. The demo and repository distinguish mock data, experimental models, local verification and unprovisioned cloud architecture. This is a reproducible engineering case study, not a live trading service.

chunks.title: Sentinance — interview-ready claims (source-backed)
chunks.heading: Case study
chunks.text: Exchange events carry identifiers and timestamps, but dashboards can easily flatten observed prices, derived indicators, forecasts and generated explanations into equally authoritative-looking values. I designed Sentinance to preserve those distinctions. The core source adapter validates aggregate-trade payloads and source-owned IDs. Kafka provides acknowledged event transport while a PostgreSQL ledger enforces duplicate-safe persistence. I added resumable local checkpoints and explicit receipt reconciliation because a broker ACK is not proof of database receipt. The ledger exports immutable raw, validated and curated Parquet snapshots with checksums. The data-model workflow loads an independently pinned snapshot into DuckDB and runs actual dbt mart builds twice to catch duplicates and stale transformations.

chunks.title: Sentinance — interview-ready claims (source-backed)
chunks.heading: Case study
chunks.text:
For forecasting, a chronological split fits ridge autoregression on log returns using only training data; validation selects regularization, and the held-out period is evaluated against last-close and moving-average baselines. The report records exact predictions, timestamps, model settings, dataset provenance and limitations. A deterministic LangGraph workflow reads a digest-pinned report, recomputes statistics and returns an explicit citation and tool-step trace; it does not call a real LLM or make investment recommendations. A read-only API and Next.js evidence page display the results. GitHub CI uses real disposable Kafka/PostgreSQL services and a Chromium test that corrupts the model artifact to prove the failure state.
The most important trade-off is deliberately leaving the public deployment, provider licensing and paid cloud services unverified. I chose a defensible synthetic golden path over invented live metrics.

chunks.title: Sentinance — interview-ready claims (source-backed)
chunks.heading: Interview story
chunks.text: Challenge: Kafka ACK does not imply a row is safely in PostgreSQL. Decision: maintain a local source cursor after ACK, detect unreceived IDs in a bounded range by checking the durable source ledger, explicitly replay missing source IDs and rely on a unique source/symbol/ID constraint for idempotency. Failure test: force a missing record; replay through Kafka; confirm the PostgreSQL row appears once and the browser does not label fixture data live. Limitation: local source checkpoint is not distributed exactly-once processing, and real exchange retention/licensing and cross-region recovery remain unproven.

chunks.title: Sentinance — interview-ready claims (source-backed)
chunks.heading: Appropriate and inappropriate claims
chunks.text:
Appropriate: exact checked synthetic CI path; actual migrated Postgres and Kafka test services; Parquet/dbt validation; digest-pinned statistical forecasts and limited LangGraph evidence; AWS infrastructure defined and offline-validated.
Inappropriate: deployed AWS services; production real-time price streaming from Binance; profitable forecasts; live LSTM accuracy, full LLM/RAG evaluation, enterprise-grade ready status, saved production cost or real user traffic. Web deployment != verified draft backend deployment.
Evidence: API CI, dbt, browser CI artifact, offline Terraform. These links verify the earlier fe44c78 branch revision, not later unverified additions.

chunks.title: RAG retrieval evaluation
chunks.text:
What is measured: the production RAGService path (add_news → Qdrant upsert → search) on a fixed, labelled, synthetic corpus. The corpus has 36 crypto-news items written for this repo and 24 paraphrased queries with 27 relevant pairs. It deliberately includes near-misses: ETF inflows vs outflows, exchange hack vs outage, approval vs rejection.
How: CI job RAG Retrieval Evaluation (Qdrant) runs apps/api/evals/rag_retrieval_eval.py against a qdrant/qdrant:v1.13.4 service container. It embeds with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 through FastEmbed, which needs no API key. Production uses Gemini embeddings, which CI can't call, so these scores describe this corpus and model, not production retrieval.

chunks.title: RAG retrieval evaluation
chunks.heading: Results (first measured run, 23 Nov 2026, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest CPU)

chunks.title: RAG retrieval evaluation
chunks.heading: Gate
chunks.text: Gate: CI fails if recall@5 < 0.90, MRR@10 < 0.90, or dense MRR is not above BM25.

chunks.title: RAG retrieval evaluation
chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text: Limits: - The corpus is small and synthetic, and the queries were written by the same author as the documents. - A Gemini-embedding run, and a larger corpus with independent query writers, would be the next steps.

Source ID / broker ack / idempotent Postgres / replay and gap detection, immutable three-layer Parquet, repeat dbt models; a single seeded end-to-end fixture test exists. Local checkpoint is not a distributed sink watermark, and live provider licensing, backfills under sustained load and provider health monitoring remain open. - P2: tested synthetic forecasting. Last-close and five-bar mean vs fitted chronological ridge AR(1), pinned manifest, train/validation/test boundaries, synthetic rolling folds and a write-once content registry. LSTM has not been shown superior; no real licensed historical evaluation, drift monitoring or model calibration is certified. New error intervals and benchmark require latest CI. - P3: constrained deterministic graph. Citation and per-step trace plus injection/refusal tests, exact one-query supported; separate conversational LLM/RAG remains optional, without reliable hosted citations or measured real-provider costs. - P4: Terraform review only.

chunks.title: Trusted ingress, Host and WebSocket Origin deployment gate
chunks.text: Status: Code and offline tests exist on draft PR #30. No production ingress or real external DNS/TLS path has been verified. This is not a release approval.

chunks.title: Trusted ingress, Host and WebSocket Origin deployment gate
chunks.heading: Required production configuration
chunks.text: Set each of these using the actual deployment topology before starting an API container with SENTINANCE_ENV=production: Variable · RequirementSENTINANCE_ENV · production or staging (both fail closed) FRONTEND_URL · Exact HTTPS browser origin, no path, e.g. an actual frontend FQDN CORS_ORIGINS · Optional additional exact HTTPS origins, comma-separated, no * SENTINANCE_ALLOWED_HOSTS · Required comma-separated exact API Host names, no protocol/port/wildcards SENTINANCE_TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS · Literal IP addresses of verified reverse-proxy peers; optional default 127.0.0.1 only PORT / API_PORT · Valid listening port, default 8000 Do not copy a fictitious domain or proxy address into deployment settings. The Docker image now launches python server.py, whose default environment is production unless a developer explicitly opts into development mode. docker-compose.yml also sets production mode and binds the API host port to 127.0.0.1, not all external interfaces. The frontend Docker port and separate public ingress must still be audited before deployment.

chunks.title: Trusted ingress, Host and WebSocket Origin deployment gate
chunks.heading: Required production configuration
chunks.text:
infra/k8s/config.yaml intentionally selects SENTINANCE_ENV=production without inventing a frontend or API FQDN. Both Kubernetes and Compose production startup must fail until FRONTEND_URL and SENTINANCE_ALLOWED_HOSTS have been populated with the real public values.
The startup program apps/api/server.py passes the parsed trusted literal peer IPs to Uvicorn's forwarded_allow_ips. Wildcards, 0.0.0.0/0, hostname entries, unspecified addresses and malformed lists are rejected. A source IP that is not trusted must not rewrite its address or scheme via X-Forwarded-For or X-Forwarded-Proto.

chunks.title: Trusted ingress, Host and WebSocket Origin deployment gate
chunks.heading: Browser/WebSocket protection
chunks.text:
HTTP CORS alone does not enforce a browser WebSocket's Origin. The /ws/prices endpoint therefore closes unapproved or missing Origin during handshake with code 1008 before accepting or allocating a manager connection. Valid origins must match the exact configured browser allowlist. The origin check is not authentication: a non-browser client can forge Origin. Additional authentication, per-user authorization and connection rate limits are separate gates before exposing private data.
Only use WSS through a TLS-terminating ingress. The ingress must forward WebSocket Upgrade headers correctly, restrict direct access to internal API ports, prevent arbitrary client-supplied forwarded headers from being trusted, and terminate TLS at a managed trust boundary.

chunks.title: Trusted ingress, Host and WebSocket Origin deployment gate
chunks.heading: Release verification (all open until real ingress tested)
chunks.text: - [ ] Establish the actual API and frontend DNS FQDNs; obtain TLS certificates. - [ ] Determine exact network-peer ingress IPs; no wildcard proxy trust. - [ ] Confirm startup fails without required production domains or with malformed/wildcard origin/Host values. - [ ] Confirm a valid HTTPS origin and Host work behind the real ingress. - [ ] Confirm unknown/missing/null WebSocket Origin is rejected before accept. - [ ] Confirm forged Host and untrusted X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto cannot change the server's routing or accepted peer identity. - [ ] Test WSS Upgrade and idle timeout across a deployed ingress and independently running API replicas. - [ ] Define per-IP and per-user connection/rate limits, authentication for protected channels, and safe logging of rejected handshakes. - [ ] Inspect final exact-head CI, security scan and operator sign-off. - [ ] Retain human approval before merge, cloud spend or production rollout.

chunks.title: Opt-in Sentinance AWS analytics sandbox (review only)
chunks.text:
This independent Terraform root is the low-cost alternative to the legacy EKS/NAT/RDS/Redis design in ../main.tf. Run commands from this directory, not the parent. Existing local PostgreSQL/Kafka ingestion and verified immutable Parquet remain the data sources. This sandbox defines a private S3 bucket (versioning, SSE-S3, TLS-only policy, public access disabled), Glue metadata database, Athena named workgroup with 1 GiB per-query cutoff, and environment-bound GitHub OIDC role scoped to approved snapshot and query-result prefixes. The role is not an infrastructure apply role. No Lambda, EventBridge, live ingestion, schema registration, Secrets Manager or backend hosting is provisioned. This is a reviewable starting point, not a deployed cloud pipeline.
Data layout: snapshots/<snapshot_id>/raw/raw.parquet, validated/validated.parquet, curated/minute_bars.parquet and manifest.json. Use fixture datasets until data rights are verified. Catalog table registration/import and checksum-preserving upload require separate approved execution. Never expose the bucket or put AWS credentials into a frontend or GitHub repository.

chunks.text:

Offline checks: terraform fmt -check -recursive; terraform init -backend=false -input=false; terraform validate. CI has no AWS credentials and does not plan or apply. Before a real plan, configure a reviewed remote state backend, unique bucket, region (default eu-west-2), valid existing GitHub OIDC provider and protected analytics-review GitHub environment with approval and branch restrictions. Obtain explicit cost/plan and deployment approval. Never apply the parent legacy template as part of this workflow. No production environment is accepted.

chunks.title: Opt-in Sentinance AWS analytics sandbox (review only)
chunks.text: Cost worksheet: Athena on-demand = scanned TB × regional price; 100 queries capped at 1 GiB each have an upper scan-volume scenario of roughly 0.1 TB (before canceled queries, charges per minimum and retries). At an illustrative $5/TB, that is about $0.5 query scanning, not a bill forecast. Add regional S3 stored GB-month + writes/reads + versioned objects and query results, Glue catalog and CloudWatch charges. No always-on compute is created. No monthly hard cap: the per-query cutoff cancels excessive queries but repeated queries still cost money. Versioning retains old objects; review lifecycle for results and noncurrent versions with owner-approved retention, and set budget notifications before applying. See Athena pricing, S3 pricing, Athena scan controls. Validate region-specific rates with AWS Pricing Calculator. No account prices or actual costs have been measured.

chunks.title: Opt-in Sentinance AWS analytics sandbox (review only)
chunks.text: Teardown requires review and separate authorization: inventory retained objects and versions, export evidence, explicitly approve deletion (force_destroy is false), then use the reviewed Terraform destruction plan. Do not delete production buckets, shared OIDC providers, or remote state. Nothing has been provisioned.

chunks.text: SENTINANCE / THE SIGNAL ATLAS: A market-intelligence engineering project exploring how raw exchange data becomes structured signals, model outputs and AI-assisted analysis. The hero is a conceptual illustration, not live prices or a trading recommendation.

The frontend's public Vercel address is not proof of a hosted Kafka/PostgreSQL/backend connection. chunks.title: Sentinance README
chunks.heading: 01 / The problem: markets generate noise
chunks.text:
Exchange feeds arrive continuously. Indicators and forecasts create more signals, while analysts still need a way to interpret them and understand which parts of a conclusion are measured, modeled or generated.
Sentinance explores one connected engineering answer: normalize market information, expose it through consistent APIs, add analytical and AI-assisted paths, then present it through a fast, readable dashboard.
Design principle: Separate the observed market data from the system's predictions and AI-generated interpretations.
